spine:n1_6327.title: SPINE ASSESSMENT FLOWCHART — LOW BACK · NECK & UPPER BACK
spine:n1_6327.sourceText:
SPINE ASSESSMENT FLOWCHART — LOW BACK · NECK & UPPER BACK
A question-by-question pathway from “my back (or neck) hurts” to a working diagnosis, an exercise group, a measured baseline and a re-test plan — using only questions, observation and hands-on tests. No imaging is assumed.
Built from: JOSPT physical therapy clinical practice guidelines (low back pain 2012 and 2021 revision, neck pain 2017), NICE NG59 (low back pain and sciatica, 2016/2020), the WHO guideline on chronic primary low back pain (2023), the IFOMPT international frameworks for spinal red flags (2020) and cervical vascular screening (2023), the Lancet Low Back Pain Series (2018), the STarT Back trial, and diagnostic accuracy studies. Draft for clinical review — a physiotherapist should sign off before use with patients.

spine:n1_6331.title: HOW TO USE THIS BOARD
spine:n1_6331.sourceText:
HOW TO USE THIS BOARD
1. Start at the black START box and follow the arrows.
2. Yellow boxes are QUESTIONS. Ask them in plain words, pick the white answer box that matches what the patient says, and follow its arrow.
3. Blue boxes are HANDS-ON CHECKS. Each one says what to do, what counts as positive, how accurate it is, and who can usually do it.
4. Every pathway runs in 4 stages: Stage 1 safety screen (is this safe to treat with exercise?) → Stage 2 working diagnosis (which problem is it?) → Stage 3 exercise group (diagnoses that share a problem share a programme) → Stage 4 measure, dose the exercise, re-test.
5. Dashed grey arrows jump to another part of the board. Grey curved arrows link each working diagnosis to its exercise group(s). Box codes (e.g. L3, LT2, ND4, LX-C) let you jump by name.

Starting assumption: the pain has been checked as musculoskeletal. But back and neck pain are the commonest disguise for heart, blood-vessel, kidney and abdominal problems, so Stage 1 re-checks them.

spine:n1_6335.title: HOW TO READ THE ACCURACY NUMBERS
spine:n1_6335.sourceText:
HOW TO READ THE ACCURACY NUMBERS
Sensitivity — out of 100 people who really HAVE the problem, how many the test catches. A highly sensitive test that comes back NEGATIVE helps rule the problem OUT.
Specificity — out of 100 people who do NOT have it, how many the test correctly clears. A highly specific test that comes back POSITIVE helps rule the problem IN.
Likelihood ratio (LR) — how strongly a result shifts the odds. LR+ above 10 = strong rule-in; LR− below 0.1 = strong rule-out; LR+ 2–5 = small shift.
Post-test probability — the chance the problem is really there once this finding is present (used for red flags, Downie 2013).
Cluster — several findings counted together; beats any single test for almost every condition here.
Consensus — expert agreement only; no accuracy study was found. Treat these boxes with more caution.
Working diagnosis — the best label you can act on without imaging. It is confirmed, or revised, by how the patient responds at the week-4 re-test.

spine:n1_6339.title: PLAIN-LANGUAGE GLOSSARY
spine:n1_6339.sourceText:
PLAIN-LANGUAGE GLOSSARY
Flexion / extension — bending forward / arching backward. Rotation / side-bending — twisting / tipping sideways.
Lumbar / thoracic / cervical — low back / mid and upper back (rib level) / neck.
Radicular pain — shooting pain along a nerve root: below the knee in the leg, below the elbow in the arm. Radiculopathy — the same plus numbness, weakness or reflex loss.
Referred pain — pain felt away from its source without nerve-root signs (e.g. back pain felt in the buttock or thigh).
Centralisation — leg or arm symptoms retreat toward the spine with a repeated movement: a good sign. Peripheralisation — they spread further out: a warning sign.
Directional preference — one direction of repeated movement (usually arching or bending) eases the pain and improves movement.
Myelopathy — pressure on the spinal cord: clumsy hands, unsteady walking.
Central sensitisation / nociplastic pain — the nervous system’s alarm is turned up; pain is widespread and out of proportion to tissue findings.
Yellow flags — beliefs, fears, mood, sleep and work factors that predict slow recovery.
Dermatome / myotome — skin area / muscle group supplied by one nerve root.
Imaging — X-ray, CT or MRI. Doctor — the medical officer on the team.

spine:n1_6343.title: WHO CAN DO EACH CHECK (guidance, never a stop)
spine:n1_6343.sourceText:
WHO CAN DO EACH CHECK (guidance, never a stop)
Anyone trained — a health worker after short training: questions, looking, pressing, simple movements.
Basic kit — needs a thermometer, tape measure, blood-pressure cuff or phone app.
Physio-level — needs a physiotherapist’s or doctor’s hands-on skill; can be done by video review or at referral.
If nobody with the skill is available: record the history, film the movement, note the test as “not done” and keep going — the pathway still works, with a little less certainty.

spine:G-Q0.sourceText:
Q0 · Where is the main pain?
ASK: “Point with one finger to where it hurts the most, then show me everywhere else you feel it.”
DO: draw it on a body chart — the drawing is reused in Stage 2 and at every re-test.

spine:G-N0B.title: Use MOVEMENT to decide
spine:G-N0B.sourceText:
Use MOVEMENT to decide
Ask them to bend, arch and twist the low back, then turn, tip and nod the head and lift both arms. The region whose movement reproduces the familiar pain is the source.
Mid-back pain that changes with breathing, twisting the chest or arm movement → NECK & UPPER BACK pathway. Pain that changes with bending and arching the low back → LOW BACK pathway.
Mid-back (thoracic) pain is itself a warning sign for fracture, cancer and TB — run the Stage 1 checks carefully.

spine:G-LB.title: LOW BACK PATHWAY
spine:G-LB.sourceText:
LOW BACK PATHWAY
Stage 1 safety screen (12 checks) → Stage 2 which low-back problem is it (12 working diagnoses) → Stage 3 exercise group (6 groups + a core programme) → Stage 4 measure, dose, re-test.

spine:LS1.title: STAGE 1 — SAFETY SCREEN: Is this back pain safe to treat with exercise?
spine:LS1.sourceText:
STAGE 1 — SAFETY SCREEN: Is this back pain safe to treat with exercise?
Ask the 12 checks in order, most time-critical first. Any YES stops the pathway and names the action. All NO → Stage 2.
Read this first: fewer than 1 in 100 people with new back pain in primary care have a serious cause, yet 80% have at least one “red flag” (Henschke 2009). A single flag on its own is weak; clusters, the whole story and change over time matter more (IFOMPT red-flag framework, Finucane 2020).

spine:n1_6559.title: SAFETY MODIFIERS — not stops; they change who signs off and how hard you start
spine:n1_6559.sourceText:
SAFETY MODIFIERS — not stops; they change who signs off and how hard you start
• Chest pain, breathlessness or fainting with effort → doctor before progressive exercise.
• Blood pressure clearly uncontrolled → doctor sign-off first (use the local cut-off).
• Pregnancy → avoid lying flat on the back after the first trimester; pelvic girdle pain is common and exercise-responsive (LD10).
• Known osteoporosis → avoid loaded bending and twisting of the spine (Group LX-F).
• Diabetes → check the feet before barefoot work.

YELLOW FLAGS — record now, score in Stage 4
• Belief that pain means damage, fear of bending, expecting to need a scan or surgery, low mood, poor sleep, worries about work or money. These predict slow recovery better than any scan or tissue label.

CONTEXT TO RECORD (changes the plan)
• Heavy manual or field work, carrying water or head-loads, long hours bent over (planting, washing clothes, sweeping), two-wheeler or auto-rickshaw driving, floor sitting and squatting toilets define the goals.

spine:L1.title: L1 · Cauda equina syndrome (pressure on the bundle of nerves at the bottom of the spine)
spine:L1.sourceText:
L1 · Cauda equina syndrome (pressure on the bundle of nerves at the bottom of the spine)
ASK (privately and plainly): NEW trouble passing urine — hard to start, weak stream, can’t tell when the bladder is full? Leaking urine or stool? Numbness between the legs or around the back passage (the “saddle” area) — e.g. can’t feel the toilet paper? NEW loss of sexual feeling or function? Sciatica in BOTH legs, or leg weakness getting worse?
CHECK: ask how they last passed urine; light touch on the inner thighs and buttocks if trained and acceptable to the patient.
EVIDENCE: urinary retention is the most consistent finding (sensitivity about 90%; Deyo 1992), but early cauda equina often shows only subtle bladder or saddle changes — act on symptoms, don’t wait for full retention. No single finding is reliable; any combination needs same-day imaging (consensus; Finucane 2020).
WHO: anyone trained
Any NEW bladder, bowel, saddle or sexual change, or sciatica in both legs?

spine:L1Y.title: EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
spine:L1Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
Same-day emergency MRI via the doctor or the nearest hospital. No exercise.
Every back-pain patient also leaves with the cauda equina warning card: come back immediately if any of these start.

spine:L2.title: L2 · Spinal fracture after major injury
spine:L2.sourceText:
L2 · Spinal fracture after major injury
ASK: Road accident, fall from a height (roof, tree, ladder, well), a heavy load falling on the back, or a kick from an animal? Can you move your legs and feel your feet?
CHECK: look for bruising or grazes over the spine; press along the bony midline for one very tender spot; check leg strength and feeling.
EVIDENCE: severe trauma raises the chance of a spinal fracture to about 11%; a bruise or graze over the spine to about 62% (post-test probabilities, Downie 2013).
WHO: anyone trained
Major injury with midline tenderness, bruising, or any leg weakness or numbness?

spine:L2Y.title: EMERGENCY
spine:L2Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY
Keep them lying flat; move the body as one unit (log-roll); emergency transfer for imaging. No exercise.

spine:L3.title: L3 · Spinal infection (bone or disc infection, epidural abscess)
spine:L3.sourceText:
L3 · Spinal infection (bone or disc infection, epidural abscess)
ASK: Fever, chills or night sweats with the back pain? A recent infection (urine, skin, chest), spinal injection or surgery? Injecting drug use, diabetes, kidney failure, HIV, steroid tablets or chemotherapy?
CHECK: temperature; firm tap (percussion) over each spinal bone for one exquisitely tender level; is the pain severe, constant and worse at night?
EVIDENCE: fever is often absent in spinal infection, so a normal temperature does NOT clear this check; the classic trio of fever, back pain and weakness is present in only a minority of epidural abscesses (consensus; Finucane 2020).
WHO: basic kit (thermometer)
Fever, OR constant severe pain with an infection risk factor?

spine:L3.decision: Fever, OR constant severe pain with an infection risk factor?

spine:L3Y.title: EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
spine:L3Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
Doctor today for blood tests (white cells, ESR/CRP) and imaging. Any new leg weakness = emergency transfer. No exercise.

spine:L4.title: L4 · Not from the spine — kidney, abdomen, pelvis or a swollen main artery (aortic aneurysm)
spine:L4.sourceText:
L4 · Not from the spine — kidney, abdomen, pelvis or a swollen main artery (aortic aneurysm)
ASK: Does the pain stay the same whatever position you take? Does it come in waves (colic), with fever, burning or blood in the urine? Linked to eating, periods, pregnancy or bleeding? An older smoker with deep central back or tummy pain? Fainting or sweating?
CHECK: do bending, arching and twisting change the pain at all? Gentle fist-tap over each kidney (the angle under the lowest rib). With the patient lying down, feel above the navel for a pulsing mass. Pulse and blood pressure.
POSITIVE IF: movement doesn’t change the pain AND any feature above is present.
NOTE: a leaking aortic aneurysm felt in the back is time-critical — older male smokers with high blood pressure are at most risk. In women who could be pregnant, early-pregnancy pain or bleeding must be ruled out (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained; basic kit (BP cuff)
Pain not changed by movement, with a kidney, abdominal, pelvic or artery sign?

spine:L4Y.title: EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
spine:L4Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
Pulsing mass, fainting, low blood pressure or sudden severe pain → emergency transfer now. Kidney or pelvic signs → same-day doctor. Not an exercise problem.

spine:L5.title: L5 · Severe or worsening nerve damage (progressive neurological deficit)
spine:L5.sourceText:
L5 · Severe or worsening nerve damage (progressive neurological deficit)
ASK: Is a leg or foot getting weaker week by week? Tripping because the foot slaps or drops? Numbness spreading?
CHECK (compare sides): walk on the heels (L4–L5) and on the toes (S1); 10 single-leg heel raises; lift the big toe against your finger (L5); knee and ankle reflexes if trained; light touch on the shin, top of the foot and outer foot.
POSITIVE IF: clear weakness (can’t heel- or toe-walk), foot drop, weakness in more than one nerve-root area, or weakness worse than at the last visit.
NOTE: a mild, STABLE deficit with sciatica is common and is NOT a stop — it goes to Stage 2 (sciatica). Progression is what matters (consensus; NICE NG59).
WHO: anyone trained (heel/toe walk); physio-level (reflexes)
Marked or worsening weakness, or foot drop?

spine:L5Y.title: URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
spine:L5Y.sourceText:
URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
Doctor or spine surgeon within days; SAME DAY if it is getting worse quickly. Keep gentle walking; no loaded exercise until reviewed.

spine:L6.title: L6 · Fragility (osteoporotic) fracture of a spinal bone
spine:L6.sourceText:
L6 · Fragility (osteoporotic) fracture of a spinal bone
ASK: Over 50 (especially a woman after menopause), or anyone over 70? Long-term steroid tablets? Sudden back pain after a minor strain, cough, sneeze, lifting a child or a small fall? Getting shorter or more stooped?
CHECK:
• Closed-fist percussion: patient standing facing a mirror; gently thump down the spine with the side of a closed fist. Sharp, sudden, fracture-like pain = positive. Sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 90% (Langdon 2010).
• Supine sign: can’t lie flat on the back on one pillow because of severe pain = positive. Sensitivity 81%, specificity 93% (Langdon 2010).
EVIDENCE: long-term steroid use raises the chance of fracture to about 33%; several red flags together to about 90% (Downie 2013). Age over 70, steroid use, significant trauma and female sex are the informative fracture flags in primary care (Henschke 2009).
WHO: anyone trained

spine:L6Y.sourceText:

Doctor for an X-ray and a bone-health review (osteoporosis medicines, calcium, vitamin D). Pain relief and gentle walking meanwhile; avoid lifting and loaded bending.
Once confirmed stable → Stage 2 box LD12 and Exercise Group LX-F (dashed arrow).

spine:L7.title: L7 · Possible cancer in the spine
spine:L7.sourceText:
L7 · Possible cancer in the spine
ASK: Have you EVER had cancer (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid, blood)? Unexplained weight loss? Pain that is constant, worse lying down or at night, eased by no position? Over 50 with a first-ever episode? Not getting better after 4–6 weeks of good care? Pain in the mid-back (rib level)?
CHECK: weigh and compare with the record; tap each spinal bone for a single tender level; look and feel for lumps.
EVIDENCE: a past history of cancer is the most useful single flag — it raises the chance of spinal cancer to about 33% (Downie 2013). Most other flags (age, night pain alone) shift the odds very little on their own.
NOTE: night pain ALONE is common in ordinary back pain. Escalate night pain that comes WITH a cancer history, weight loss, constant pain or no improvement.
WHO: anyone trained

spine:L7Y.sourceText:
URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
Doctor for blood tests and imaging before any loading exercise. Any leg weakness or bladder change → L1 / L5, same day.

spine:L8.title: L8 · Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
spine:L8.sourceText:
L8 · Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
ASK: Back pain for weeks to months that keeps getting worse? Night sweats, evening fevers, cough, weight loss, poor appetite? TB now or in the past, or in the family? HIV or diabetes?
CHECK: look from the side for a sharp, angled hump (gibbus); tap each spinal bone for one tender level; a stiff spine held by muscle spasm; leg strength (L5).
NOTE: the spine is the commonest site of bone and joint TB (about half of cases), usually the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine; delay risks collapse of the spine and paralysis (osteoarticular TB review, 2020). In TB-endemic areas keep a low threshold.
WHO: anyone trained
Worsening back pain with TB features, or a gibbus?

spine:L8Y.title: URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
spine:L8Y.sourceText:
URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
Doctor for a TB work-up (blood tests, chest X-ray, spine imaging). No loading exercise or manipulation until assessed. Leg weakness → same day.

spine:L9.title: L9 · Child or teenager with back pain
spine:L9.sourceText:
L9 · Child or teenager with back pain
ASK: Under 18? Pain for more than 4 weeks? Night pain, fever, weight loss? A stiff, curved spine or a limp? A sporty teenager (cricket fast-bowling, gymnastics, dance, weight-lifting, wrestling) whose pain is worse when ARCHING backwards?
CHECK: forward-bend test — look from behind for a rib hump (scoliosis) and from the side for a sharp angled hump; is the curve painful and rigid? Stand on one leg and arch back (stork test): pain on the standing side?
NOTE: in children, back pain more often has a structural cause than in adults. In young athletes with pain on arching, a stress fracture at the back of a vertebra (spondylolysis) is common — but the stork test is not accurate enough to rule it in or out (Grødahl 2016); imaging decides.
WHO: anyone trained
Child with a warning sign, or a teen athlete with pain on arching?

spine:L10.title: L10 · Inflammatory back pain (axial spondyloarthritis)
spine:L10.sourceText:
L10 · Inflammatory back pain (axial spondyloarthritis)
ASK — the ASAS inflammatory back pain criteria (count them): (1) started before age 40; (2) came on gradually; (3) gets better with exercise; (4) does NOT get better with rest; (5) pain at night that eases on getting up.
Also: morning stiffness over 30 minutes? Alternating buttock pain? Psoriasis, bowel disease, a red painful eye, a swollen heel or a “sausage” finger or toe? Family history?
POSITIVE IF: 4 or more of the 5.
EVIDENCE: 4 of 5 = sensitivity 77%, specificity 92% in the expert cohort; 80% and 72% in the validation cohort (Sieper 2009).

spine:L10Y.sourceText:

spine:L11.title: L11 · Pain coming from the hip (or from the hip AND the back)
spine:L11.sourceText:
L11 · Pain coming from the hip (or from the hip AND the back)
ASK: Groin pain? Pain putting on socks or shoes, getting out of a vehicle, or sitting cross-legged on the floor? A limp?
CHECK: lying on the back, bend the hip to 90° and turn it in and out; compare sides. Does this reproduce the familiar pain while back movements don’t?
POSITIVE IF: hip movement reproduces the pain; back movement doesn’t.
NOTE: hip osteoarthritis and back pain often coexist in older adults (“hip–spine syndrome”); groin pain with painful, limited inward hip rotation points to the hip (consensus).
WHO: physio-level (hip rotation); anyone trained (history)

spine:L12.sourceText:

NOTE: nerve-related claudication from spinal stenosis eases only with SITTING or BENDING FORWARD; artery-related claudication eases with standing still. Some people have both (consensus).

spine:LS2.title: STAGE 2 — WHICH LOW-BACK PROBLEM IS IT?
spine:LS2.sourceText:
STAGE 2 — WHICH LOW-BACK PROBLEM IS IT?
For most people no exact tissue can be named, and naming one wouldn’t change care (Lancet Low Back Pain Series 2018). So this stage sorts people by HOW their pain behaves — where it spreads, which repeated movement eases it, how long it has lasted, how widespread it is — because that is what picks the exercise group (JOSPT CPG; treatment-based classification, Alrwaily 2016).

spine:LQ1.title: LQ1 · Where do the symptoms go? (use the body chart from Q0)
spine:LQ1.sourceText:
LQ1 · Where do the symptoms go? (use the body chart from Q0)
ASK: “Show me everywhere you feel it. Does anything shoot down the leg? Any numbness or pins and needles?”

fields.ASK: “Show me everywhere you feel it. Does anything shoot down the leg? Any numbness or pins and needles?”

options.label: Back and/or buttock, maybe the thigh — nothing below the knee
Shooting pain below the knee into the foot, often with numbness or pins and needles
One or both legs heavy, aching or numb when standing or walking; eased by sitting or bending forward
One-sided pain low over the back of the pelvis, below the belt line; pregnant, recently delivered, or after a fall on the buttock
Pain in many places — back plus neck, shoulders, arms or legs; “everything hurts”

spine:LT1.title: LT1 · Repeated-movement test — is there a DIRECTIONAL PREFERENCE?
spine:LT1.sourceText:
LT1 · Repeated-movement test — is there a DIRECTIONAL PREFERENCE?
• Record a baseline first: where the pain reaches, how bad (0–10), how far they can bend and arch.
• Arching (extension): lying face down, push up on the hands keeping the hips down (prone press-up) × 10; or standing back-bends × 10 if they can’t lie down.
• Bending (flexion): lying on the back, pull both knees to the chest × 10; or seated forward bend × 10.
• Visible shift: glide the hips back to the middle against a wall × 10, then retest.
• After each set, re-check where the pain reaches, how bad, and how far they move.
POSITIVE (preference) IF: one direction makes buttock or thigh pain retreat toward the middle of the back (CENTRALISE) or disappear, eases the pain and improves movement — and keeps doing so set after set.
EVIDENCE: a directional preference was found in 74% of people with back pain, and exercise matched to it beat both the opposite direction and general exercise on every outcome (Long 2004, 312 patients). Centralisation also predicts a good outcome.
WHO: anyone trained (do it); physio-level (interpret unclear cases)

Bending (flexion) eases it — standing, walking and arching are usually what hurt

spine:LD1.title: LD1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Low back pain with a directional preference for EXTENSION (centralising back pain)
spine:LD1.sourceText:
LD1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Low back pain with a directional preference for EXTENSION (centralising back pain)
WHAT IT IS: back pain, often spreading to the buttock or thigh, that eases and centralises with repeated arching. Usually worse with sitting, bending and lifting; better walking. Often called “disc-related”, though that can’t be confirmed without imaging — and doesn’t need to be.
NEXT STEP: repeated extension in the direction that centralises, 10 reps every 2–3 hours, progressing from lying to standing; short sitting bouts with a lumbar roll; then load up through the core programme.
AVOID (for now): long slumped sitting and repeated loaded bending.
PROGRESS WHEN: pain stays central and bending returns — bending is reintroduced gradually, not banned for life.
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-A (extension branch)
STAGE 4 MODULE: back module.

spine:LD2.title: LD2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Low back pain with a directional preference for FLEXION (extension-intolerant back pain)
spine:LD2.sourceText:
LD2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Low back pain with a directional preference for FLEXION (extension-intolerant back pain)
WHAT IT IS: pain eased by bending forward or sitting, provoked by standing, walking far, arching or lying on the stomach. Commoner in older adults; often blamed on the small facet joints or narrowing, but no bedside test confirms a single tissue.
NEXT STEP: flexion-biased exercise (knees-to-chest, pelvic tilts, seated bending), hip-flexor stretch and hip-extensor strength, then trunk strength and walking with planned rests.
AVOID (for now): sustained arching and long standing without breaks.
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-A (flexion branch)
STAGE 4 MODULE: back module.

spine:LQ2.title: LQ2 · How long has this episode lasted, and how does it behave?
spine:LQ2.sourceText:
LQ2 · How long has this episode lasted, and how does it behave?
ASK: “When did this episode start? Has it happened before? What happens when you bend down and come back up?”

fields.ASK: “When did this episode start? Has it happened before? What happens when you bend down and come back up?”

options.label: Under 6 weeks, first or occasional episode; stiff, guarded, sore to move in all directions
Keeps coming back; “catches”, “gives way” or locks when bending or coming back up; feels better in a belt
More than 3 months; mainly in the back; worse with activity and long sitting

spine:LD3.title: LD3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Acute low back pain with mobility deficits (“acute lumbago”)
spine:LD3.sourceText:
LD3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Acute low back pain with mobility deficits (“acute lumbago”)
WHAT IT IS: a recent, stiff, painful back with no leg symptoms below the knee and no nerve signs. Most episodes improve a lot within 6 weeks.
NEXT STEP: reassurance that it is not damage; stay active and keep working where possible (bed rest slows recovery); heat wrap; gentle movement in all directions within comfort; short walks. A physio may add spinal manipulation: with symptoms for under 16 days and none below the knee, a fast response is more likely (prediction rule — Flynn 2002, 4 of 5 items LR+ 24.4; validated in an RCT with number needed to treat 1.9, Childs 2004). Later studies found the rule weaker elsewhere, so treat it as a guide.
AVOID: bed rest, braces or corsets, scans “just to check” (NICE NG59).
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-B (move early)
STAGE 4 MODULE: back module (irritability is usually HIGH at first).

spine:LT4.title: LT4 · Movement-control check — does the back move in a jerky, poorly controlled way?
spine:LT4.sourceText:
LT4 · Movement-control check — does the back move in a jerky, poorly controlled way?
• Watch bending forward and returning upright: a painful arc, a sudden “catch”, walking the hands up the thighs to stand (Gowers sign), or a reversed rhythm (hips straighten first, then the back) = aberrant movement.
• Prone instability test (physio-level): lying face down over the end of a bed, feet on the floor; press on each low-back vertebra. Then lift the feet slightly (back muscles switch on) and press again. Pain that DISAPPEARS when the muscles switch on = positive.
• Prediction rule — likely to respond to stabilisation exercise if 3 or more of: age under 40; straight-leg raise over 91°; aberrant movement; positive prone instability test (Hicks 2005: LR+ 4.0 for success).
WHO: anyone trained (watch movement); physio-level (prone instability test)

• Watch bending forward and returning upright: a painful arc, a sudden “catch”, walking the hands up the thighs to stand (Gowers sign), or a reversed rhythm (hips straighten first, then the back) = aberrant movement.

options.label: Aberrant movement, or prone instability test positive
Moves smoothly; tests negative → treat as persistent non-specific back pain (LD5)

spine:LD4.title: LD4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Low back pain with movement-control impairment (recurrent, “unstable-feeling” back)
spine:LD4.sourceText:
LD4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Low back pain with movement-control impairment (recurrent, “unstable-feeling” back)
WHAT IT IS: repeated episodes with catching or giving way and poor control of bending and lifting — the problem is how the trunk is controlled under load, not one damaged tissue. Also the home for a stable degenerative slip (spondylolisthesis) and a healed or stable pars fracture after imaging (from L9).
NEXT STEP: motor-control (stabilisation) exercise — learn to brace, then bird-dog, side-bridge and curl-up progressions, hip-hinge practice, then strength under load and work-task practice. Motor control works about as well as other active exercise, so choose what the patient will keep doing (Owen 2020).
AVOID: passive treatment alone; relying on a belt long-term.
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-C (motor control & trunk–hip strength)
STAGE 4 MODULE: back module.

spine:LD5.title: LD5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic (persistent) non-specific low back pain
spine:LD5.sourceText:
LD5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic (persistent) non-specific low back pain
WHAT IT IS: back pain on most days for more than 3 months, with no serious cause and no nerve-root signs. The back has become sensitive and deconditioned, and worry, sleep, mood and work strongly shape the pain. The commonest label in this pathway.
NEXT STEP: a structured exercise programme is the first-line treatment (NICE NG59; WHO 2023; JOSPT 2021). Any type the patient enjoys and will keep doing — strengthening, motor control, Pilates- or yoga-type, walking or other aerobic exercise — works about equally (Hayden 2021: about 15 points less pain on a 0–100 scale than no treatment or usual care; Owen 2020). Combine with education (hurt ≠ harm), pacing and graded return to valued activities. If the STarT Back score is HIGH, use the psychologically informed approach in Stage 4.
AVOID: imaging, traction, TENS, ultrasound, belts or corsets, passive treatment on its own, opioids (NICE NG59; WHO 2023).
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-E (graded activity & conditioning)
STAGE 4 MODULE: back module + yellow-flag module.

spine:LT2.title: LT2 · Nerve-root check (sciatica)
spine:LT2.sourceText:
LT2 · Nerve-root check (sciatica)
• Straight-leg raise (SLR): lying on the back, lift the straight leg slowly. Positive if it reproduces the LEG pain (not just a hamstring pull) between about 30° and 70°. Sensitivity 91%, specificity 26% — a NEGATIVE SLR helps rule disc-related nerve-root pain OUT (Devillé 2000).
• Crossed SLR: lifting the GOOD leg reproduces pain in the bad leg. Specificity 88% — a positive result helps rule it IN (Devillé 2000).
• Slump test: sitting slumped, chin to chest, straighten the knee and pull the foot up; positive if the leg pain is reproduced and eases when the head comes up. Sensitivity 84%, specificity 83% (Majlesi 2008).
• Neurological screen (compare sides): L4 — knee reflex, inner-shin feeling, heel walking; L5 — big-toe lift, top-of-foot feeling; S1 — ankle reflex, toe walking and heel raises, outer-foot feeling.
WHO: anyone trained (SLR, heel/toe walk); physio-level (slump, reflexes)

spine:LQ3.title: LQ3 · Does repeated arching bring the leg pain back up toward the back?
spine:LQ3.sourceText:
LQ3 · Does repeated arching bring the leg pain back up toward the back?
DO: run the repeated-movement test (LT1) with extra care; stop at once if the leg pain spreads further down.

fields.DO: run the repeated-movement test (LT1) with extra care; stop at once if the leg pain spreads further down.

options.label: Yes — the leg pain retreats toward the back
No change, or it spreads further down (stop that direction)

spine:LD6.title: LD6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Sciatica (lumbar radicular pain) that CENTRALISES
spine:LD6.sourceText:
LD6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Sciatica (lumbar radicular pain) that CENTRALISES
WHAT IT IS: an irritated nerve root (usually from a disc bulge at L4–5 or L5–S1) whose leg pain retreats with repeated arching. Centralisation is a good sign; most people recover without surgery, and disc bulges commonly shrink over months.
NEXT STEP: repeated extension in the centralising direction (as LD1), positions of ease, keep walking; once the leg pain has centralised, add nerve sliders and then the core programme.
AVOID: any exercise that pushes pain further down the leg; long sitting; heavy lifting in the first weeks.
REFER IF: not improving by 6–8 weeks, severe pain despite medicines, or any new weakness (NICE NG59).
EXERCISE GROUPS: LX-A (extension branch) → LX-D
STAGE 4 MODULE: sciatica module.

spine:LD7.title: LD7 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Sciatica (lumbar radicular pain / radiculopathy) — NOT centralising
spine:LD7.sourceText:
LD7 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Sciatica (lumbar radicular pain / radiculopathy) — NOT centralising
WHAT IT IS: nerve-root pain below the knee, often with pins and needles or mild stable weakness, that no repeated direction centralises. The outlook is still favourable for most within about 3 months.
NEXT STEP: calm the nerve: positions of ease (lying on the back with the calves on a chair; side-lying with a pillow between the knees), short frequent walks, nerve sliders (gentle back-and-forth nerve movement without stretching), then gradual trunk and leg strengthening. Pain medicines through the doctor.
AVOID: holding long nerve or hamstring stretches; anything that increases numbness or spreads the pain.
REFER IF: worsening weakness (L5), or severe pain at 6–8 weeks despite good care — spinal injection or surgery may then be considered (NICE NG59).
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-D (nerve-friendly)
STAGE 4 MODULE: sciatica module.

spine:LT5.title: LT5 · Spinal stenosis check (narrowing that squeezes the nerves when standing upright) — Suri 2010 review
spine:LT5.sourceText:
LT5 · Spinal stenosis check (narrowing that squeezes the nerves when standing upright) — Suri 2010 review
ASK / OBSERVE (likelihood ratios):
• No pain when sitting — LR+ 7.4
• Symptoms improve when bending forward (leaning on a trolley, walking stick or bicycle handlebars) — LR+ 6.4
• Pain in both buttocks or legs — LR+ 6.3
• Neurogenic claudication (leg pain, heaviness or numbness that comes with walking or standing and eases with sitting) — LR+ 3.7; its ABSENCE makes stenosis unlikely (LR− 0.23)
• Wide-based gait — LR+ 13; abnormal Romberg (feet together, eyes closed: sways or steps) — LR+ 4.2
• Age under 60 makes it less likely (LR 0.40)
WALK TEST: time upright walking on the flat, then walking leaning forward on a stick or trolley — a longer distance when leaning forward supports stenosis (two-stage treadmill idea, Fritz 1997).
ALSO: feel the foot pulses — weak pulses and relief by just standing still point to the arteries instead (L12).
WHO: anyone trained; physio-level (Romberg in unsteady older adults)

spine:LD8.title: LD8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
spine:LD8.sourceText:
LD8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
WHAT IT IS: age-related narrowing of the spinal canal; the nerves are squeezed more when standing upright and walking, less when bending forward or sitting. Walking distance is the key limit.
NEXT STEP: flexion-biased exercise, stationary cycling (usually well tolerated because it is done bent forward), a walking programme with planned rests or a stick or trolley to build distance, hip and leg strengthening, balance work. In surgical candidates, physiotherapy gave similar 2-year physical function to surgery — though 57% of the physiotherapy group later crossed over to surgery (Delitto 2015).
AVOID: long standing and prolonged arching.
REFER IF: walking distance keeps shrinking, any bladder change (L1), or worsening weakness (L5).
EXERCISE GROUPS: LX-A (flexion branch) + LX-E (walking programme)
STAGE 4 MODULE: stenosis module.

spine:LT6.title: LT6 · Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) and pelvic girdle check
spine:LT6.sourceText:
LT6 · Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) and pelvic girdle check
• Point test: the patient points to the pain — just below the bony dimple at the back of the pelvis supports the SIJ.
• Pain provocation tests (Laslett cluster): distraction (lying on the back, press the front pelvic bones apart), thigh thrust (hip bent to 90°, push down along the thigh), compression (side-lying, press down on the pelvis), sacral thrust (lying face down, press on the sacrum), Gaenslen (one hip bent up, the other leg hanging off the bed) on both sides.
POSITIVE IF: 3 or more of the 6 (or 2 of the first 4) reproduce the familiar pain: sensitivity 94%, specificity 78%. If NONE provokes the pain, the SIJ can be ruled out (Laslett 2005).
• Pregnancy or after birth: add the active straight-leg raise (lying on the back, lift one straight leg 20 cm; “heavy” or hard on one side = positive; sensitivity 87%, specificity 94%, Mens 2001) and the posterior pelvic pain provocation (thigh thrust) test (European pelvic girdle guideline, Vleeming 2008).
WHO: physio-level (provocation tests); anyone trained (active straight-leg raise)

spine:LD10.title: LD10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain
spine:LD10.sourceText:
LD10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain
WHAT IT IS: pain at the back of the pelvis and/or over the pubic bone during pregnancy or after delivery; affects about 1 in 5 pregnant women (Vleeming 2008). Not harmful to the baby; usually settles within months of the birth.
NEXT STEP: reassurance and education; individualised exercise for trunk and pelvic control (gentle bracing with a pelvic-floor squeeze, side-lying hip work, supported squats, bridges if comfortable); pacing; a pelvic belt for short-term relief; a pillow between the knees in bed; keep the knees together getting in and out of bed or a vehicle.
AVOID: lying flat on the back after the first trimester; wide-legged positions and heavy lifting while painful.
REFER IF: pain stops her walking; any bleeding, contractions or reduced baby movements → obstetric team the same day.
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-C (pelvic girdle branch)
STAGE 4 MODULE: pelvic girdle module.

spine:LD9.title: LD9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Sacroiliac joint pain
spine:LD9.sourceText:
LD9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Sacroiliac joint pain
WHAT IT IS: pain from the joint between the base of the spine (sacrum) and the pelvis — one-sided, below the belt line, often after a fall on the buttock, a missed step, or lifting with a twist.
NEXT STEP: load-transfer exercise: bracing, bridges, side-lying and standing hip abduction, hip extension, single-leg stance and step-ups; then the core programme. A pelvic belt can ease pain short-term while strength builds (consensus).
AVOID: long one-legged standing and lopsided heavy carrying while it is irritable.
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-C (pelvic girdle branch)
STAGE 4 MODULE: back module.

fields.WHAT IT IS: pain from the joint between the base of the spine (sacrum) and the pelvis — one-sided, below the belt line, often after a fall on the buttock, a missed step, or lifting with a twist.
fields.NEXT STEP: load-transfer exercise: bracing, bridges, side-lying and standing hip abduction, hip extension, single-leg stance and step-ups; then the core programme. A pelvic belt can ease pain short-term while strength builds (consensus).
fields.AVOID: long one-legged standing and lopsided heavy carrying while it is irritable.

spine:LT7.title: LT7 · Widespread pain / central sensitisation check
spine:LT7.sourceText:
LT7 · Widespread pain / central sensitisation check
• Clinical criteria (all 3): (1) pain out of proportion to the injury or findings; (2) pain spread widely or not following anatomy (both sides, many areas); (3) over-sensitive to touch, pressure, light, sound, cold or stress (Nijs 2015).
• Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI): a score of 40 or more out of 100 suggests central sensitisation (sensitivity 81%, specificity 75%; Neblett 2013).
• Re-check the inflammatory screen (L10); over 50 with shoulder- and hip-girdle stiffness → polymyalgia (neck pathway, N5).
WHO: anyone trained (questions); physio-level (interpretation)

spine:LD11.title: LD11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic back pain with widespread pain / central sensitisation (nociplastic pain)
spine:LD11.sourceText:
LD11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic back pain with widespread pain / central sensitisation (nociplastic pain)
WHAT IT IS: the nervous system’s alarm is turned up: pain spreads, flares easily and is out of proportion to any tissue problem. Includes fibromyalgia-type presentations. The pain is real — not imagined, and not damage.
NEXT STEP: pain education first (how a sensitive alarm system works); then graded activity and graded exposure to feared movements, regular aerobic exercise (walking, cycling) starting low and building slowly, sleep and stress strategies; psychological support (CBT-based) where available. Combined physical and psychological programmes are recommended (NICE NG59).
AVOID: chasing a tissue cause with repeated scans; long rest after flares; passive-only care; opioids.
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-E (graded activity & conditioning)
STAGE 4 MODULE: yellow-flag module.

spine:n1_6567.title: WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T)
spine:n1_6567.sourceText:
WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T)
For most back pain the tissue label doesn’t change care. What changes care is the PATTERN: which direction eases it, whether a nerve root is involved, whether movement control is poor, and how high the yellow flags are. So Stage 2 picks the exercise group, the directions to favour and avoid, and the starting dose — not a custom exercise list per patient.
Lateral shift: if the trunk is visibly shifted sideways and bending is blocked, correct the shift first (side-glide against a wall), then test arching. A shift usually belongs with LD1 or LD6 (consensus).

spine:LD12.title: LD12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Stable osteoporotic vertebral fracture (entry only after medical clearance — from L6)
spine:LD12.sourceText:
LD12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Stable osteoporotic vertebral fracture (entry only after medical clearance — from L6)
WHAT IT IS: a healed or stable compression fracture of a weakened vertebra, confirmed by the doctor, with bone-health treatment started.
NEXT STEP: back-extensor strengthening (lying face-down lifts, seated back extension), posture training, balance and fall-prevention exercise, progressive leg and hip strength, daily walking. Women who strengthened their back extensors had 2.7 times fewer new vertebral fractures over 10 years (Sinaki 2002). Supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training raised spine bone density without fractures in women with low bone mass (Watson 2018) — specialist-led only.
AVOID: loaded forward bending and twisting — sit-ups, toe touches, lifting from the floor with a rounded back (Too Fit To Fracture, Giangregorio 2014).
EXERCISE GROUP: LX-F (bone-safe back strength)
STAGE 4 MODULE: bone-health module.

spine:n1_6763.title: STAGE 3 — EXERCISE GROUPS: diagnoses that share a problem share a programme
spine:n1_6763.sourceText:
STAGE 3 — EXERCISE GROUPS: diagnoses that share a problem share a programme
Each working diagnosis points (grey curved arrows) to one or two groups. A group = the shared mechanism + the exercises that target it + how to progress. Pick 3–5 exercises from the group, not all of them, and set the dose in Stage 4. Everyone finishes in the CORE PROGRAMME.
Why groups work: no single exercise type beats the others for chronic back pain (Hayden 2021; Owen 2020) — matching the direction of movement (Long 2004), the patient’s preference and a progressive dose matters more than the exact exercise.

spine:LX-B.title: LX-B · Early movement & mobility (“move it gently, don’t rest it”)
spine:LX-B.sourceText:
LX-B · Early movement & mobility (“move it gently, don’t rest it”)
For: LD3 acute low back pain with mobility deficits (and any HIGH-irritability start)
SHARED PROBLEM: a sore, guarded, stiff back where fear and protective spasm limit movement; recovery is faster when people stay active.
• Walking: short bouts of 5–10 min several times a day, a little longer each day
• Cat–camel on hands and knees: 10 slow reps
• Knee rolls side to side lying on the back: 10 each way
• Pelvic tilts and gentle knees-to-chest: 10 reps
• Child’s pose / prayer stretch (sit back onto the heels): 3 × 20 s
• Heat wrap before moving if it helps (short-term relief, French 2006)
DOSE: little and often — every 2–3 hours; mild-to-moderate pain while moving is OK.
PROGRESS: within 1–2 weeks → LX-C or the core programme; return to work early on modified duties.
EVIDENCE: advice to stay active is recommended over bed rest (NICE NG59).

spine:LX-A.title: LX-A · Direction-specific repeated movements
spine:LX-A.sourceText:
LX-A · Direction-specific repeated movements
For: LD1 extension preference · LD2 flexion preference · LD6 centralising sciatica · LD8 spinal stenosis
SHARED PROBLEM: pain that changes with one direction of movement; repeating the “good” direction calms it and restores movement.
EXTENSION BRANCH (LD1, LD6):
• Lying face down, relaxed, 2–3 min → propped on the elbows, 2–3 min
• Prone press-ups: 10 reps, hips stay down, straighten the arms as able
• Standing back-bends, hands on the hips: 10 reps (use at work or in the field)
• Sitting tall with a rolled towel behind the low back
FLEXION BRANCH (LD2, LD8):
• Knees-to-chest lying on the back: 10 reps or hold 20–30 s
• Pelvic tilts (flatten the back into the floor): 10 reps
• Seated forward bend between the knees: 10 reps
• Stationary cycling, or walking leaning on a stick or trolley
DOSE: 10 reps every 2–3 hours while symptoms are active.
RULE: keep going if leg symptoms move toward the back; STOP if they spread further down the leg.
PROGRESS: pain stays central → reintroduce the opposite direction gently → core programme.

spine:LX-F.title: LX-F · Bone-safe back-extensor strength & balance
spine:LX-F.sourceText:
LX-F · Bone-safe back-extensor strength & balance
For: LD12 stable osteoporotic vertebral fracture · older adults with a stooped (hyperkyphotic) back
SHARED PROBLEM: a weak, stooped back with fragile bones — the goals are extensor strength, upright posture and fewer falls.
• Lying face down (pillow under the tummy): lift the head and chest a little, 8–10 reps, hold 3 s
• Seated back extension against a chair back, shoulder blades squeezed: 10 reps
• Wall stand — heels, buttocks, shoulders and head toward the wall: 5 × 10 s
• Sit-to-stand and mini squats with a hip-hinge (no rounding); heel raises
• Balance: tandem stance and heel-to-toe walking beside a support
• Daily walking
AVOID: sit-ups, toe touches, twisting with load, lifting from the floor with a rounded back.
EVIDENCE: back-extensor exercise → 2.7 times fewer vertebral fractures at 10 years (Sinaki 2002); exercise guidance from Too Fit To Fracture (Giangregorio 2014).

spine:LX-D.title: LX-D · Nerve-friendly movement (calm the nerve, then load it)
spine:LX-D.sourceText:
LX-D · Nerve-friendly movement (calm the nerve, then load it)
For: LD7 non-centralising sciatica · LD6 centralising sciatica (once the leg pain has centralised)
SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitive, irritated nerve root that dislikes being stretched or squeezed but improves with gentle movement and blood flow.
• Positions of ease: lying with the calves on a chair; side-lying with a pillow between the knees
• Seated nerve slider: sitting tall, straighten the knee while looking up, then bend the knee while looking down — 10–15 smooth reps, no stretch pain
• Lying slider: hold behind the thigh; straighten and bend the knee while pointing and pulling up the foot — 10 reps
• Short walks several times a day
• Then rebuild the muscles of that nerve root: bridges, sit-to-stand, step-ups, heel raises
DOSE: sliders 10–15 reps, 2–3 times a day; any symptoms must settle within minutes.
RULE: numbness or pain spreading further down = too much — stop and step down.
AVOID: holding long hamstring or “sciatic” stretches.
EVIDENCE: neural mobilisation reduced pain (about 1.8 points out of 10) and disability in chronic low back pain (Basson 2017).

spine:LX-C.title: LX-C · Motor control & trunk–hip strength
spine:LX-C.sourceText:
LX-C · Motor control & trunk–hip strength
For: LD4 movement-control impairment (incl. stable slip, healed pars fracture) · LD9 sacroiliac joint pain · LD10 pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain
SHARED PROBLEM: the trunk and pelvis don’t control load well — catching, giving way, or pain when weight passes through the pelvis.
• Bracing — gently tighten the tummy and pelvic floor, keep breathing: 10 × 10 s
• Bird-dog on hands and knees, opposite arm and leg: 6–10 each side, hold 5–10 s
• Side-bridge from the knees → from the feet: 3–5 × 10 s each side
• Curl-up, hands under the low back, head and shoulders only: 5–10 × 10 s
• Bridges: 10–15 reps → single-leg bridges
• Hip-hinge with a stick along the spine → lift a light load from chair height
PELVIC GIRDLE BRANCH (LD9, LD10): side-lying leg lifts, clams, standing hip extension, single-leg stance holding a support, step-ups; pelvic belt short-term; in pregnancy use side-lying and hands-and-knees versions instead of lying flat.
DOSE: holds 6–10 × 10 s once or twice daily → 2–3 sets of 8–12 under load.
EVIDENCE: motor control / stabilisation is among the most effective exercise types for chronic back pain (Owen 2020); the Hicks 2005 rule picks likely responders.

spine:LX-E.title: LX-E · Graded activity, aerobic conditioning & pain education
spine:LX-E.sourceText:
LX-E · Graded activity, aerobic conditioning & pain education
For: LD5 chronic non-specific back pain · LD11 widespread pain / central sensitisation · LD8 stenosis (walking programme) · anyone with a HIGH STarT Back score
SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitised, deconditioned system and fear of movement — the aim is confidence and capacity, not finding “the right muscle”.
• Pain education: hurt ≠ harm; flare-ups are expected and settle
• Walking programme: start at 70–80% of today’s comfortable time or distance; add about 10% a week (by plan, not by pain)
• Graded exposure: list feared activities (bending, lifting, floor sitting) and practise them in small, safe steps
• Whole-body strength: sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, rows with a band or water bottles, step-ups
• Yoga- or Pilates-style classes, tai chi, cycling, swimming — whatever they enjoy
• Relaxed breathing and a regular sleep routine
DOSE: build toward 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus 2 strength days (WHO 2020 physical activity guidelines).
RULE: progress by the plan (time-contingent), not by how the pain feels that day.
EVIDENCE: exercise reduces pain in chronic back pain with no clear best type (Hayden 2021); stratified, psychologically informed care improved disability and saved costs (Hill 2011).

spine:LX-CORE.title: LX-CORE · CORE PROGRAMME FOR EVERYONE — where every group ends up
spine:LX-CORE.sourceText:
LX-CORE · CORE PROGRAMME FOR EVERYONE — where every group ends up
Once symptoms are settling, every patient moves here. For chronic back pain the evidence favours any well-dosed, enjoyable, progressive programme over the “perfect” exercise.
STRENGTH (2–3 days a week, 2–3 sets of 8–12): sit-to-stand → squat holding a water pot; hip-hinge → lifting a sack or bag from a step; split squats or step-ups; rows with a band; carrying practice (two equal loads, then one-sided).
ENDURANCE: walking, cycling or swimming, building to 150 minutes a week.
WORK AND LIFE TASKS: practise the patient’s own PSFS goals — floor sitting and rising, squatting toilet, lifting a child, carrying water, field-work postures, riding a two-wheeler.
FLARE-UP PLAN: drop back one level for 2–3 days, keep walking, use the group’s easing movement, then rebuild.
WHY KEEP GOING: 69% of people have another episode within 12 months of recovering (da Silva 2019); exercise with education cut the risk of a new episode by about 45% (Steffens 2016).

spine:LS4.title: STAGE 4 — MEASURE, DOSE THE EXERCISE, RE-TEST
spine:LS4.sourceText:
STAGE 4 — MEASURE, DOSE THE EXERCISE, RE-TEST
Every patient comes here from their exercise group. Everyone gets the same short core battery so results compare across patients and visits; the diagnosis adds one module; irritability (not the label) sets the starting dose; the STarT Back score sets HOW the programme is delivered.

spine:LS4-1.title: LS4-1 · How irritable is the back?
spine:LS4-1.sourceText:
LS4-1 · How irritable is the back?
ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours and about sleep too.

fields.ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours and about sleep too.

options.label: HIGH: pain at rest or wakes you; small movements flare it; takes hours or until the next day to settle
MODERATE: pain with some activities; settles within an hour or two
LOW: pain only with heavy or long activity; settles within minutes

spine:LS4-HI.title: START GENTLE
spine:LS4-HI.sourceText:
START GENTLE
Positions of ease, the group’s easing movement (LX-A or LX-B), short walks, education. Baseline limited to pain, PSFS and the STarT Back tool.

spine:LS4-MD.sourceText:
START MODERATE
Group exercises at full dose and progressive strengthening within the pain rules. Full core battery.

spine:LS4-LO.title: START STRONGER
spine:LS4-LO.sourceText:
START STRONGER
Core programme loading, lifting and carrying practice, return to sport or heavy work tasks. Full core battery.

spine:LS4-2.title: LS4-2 · STarT Back screening tool (9 questions, about 2 minutes)
spine:LS4-2.sourceText:
LS4-2 · STarT Back screening tool (9 questions, about 2 minutes)
Scores the risk of a poor outcome from yellow flags and spreading pain. Total 0–3 = LOW risk; total 4 or more → look at the 5 psychological items: 3 or less = MEDIUM, 4–5 = HIGH (Hill 2008).
• LOW: advice, reassurance, the group’s exercises at home; 1–2 contacts.
• MEDIUM: a physiotherapy-led exercise programme (about 6 sessions).
• HIGH: psychologically informed physiotherapy — tackle fears and beliefs, graded exposure, pacing, goal-setting; involve a counsellor or doctor for low mood.
Stratified care improved disability at 4 and 12 months and saved costs compared with usual best care (Hill 2011, 851 patients).

spine:LS4-3.title: LS4-3 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes)
spine:LS4-3.sourceText:
LS4-3 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes)
Needs: a chair, a stopwatch, 10 m of floor and a phone. Repeat the SAME set at week 0, 4 and 12.
1. Pain 0–10 (faces version for low literacy): average and worst in the last week; leg pain scored separately if present.
2. Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS): the patient names their 3 hardest tasks and rates each 0–10 — this becomes the goal list. Prompt with local tasks: floor sitting and rising, squatting toilet, bending to sweep or wash clothes, carrying water or head-loads, field work, riding a two-wheeler, lifting a child.
3. Disability questionnaire: Roland-Morris (24 items) or the Oswestry Disability Index — check for a validated Hindi or Marathi version.
4. Body chart: where the symptoms reach — watch for centralisation across visits.
5. Movement: fingertip-to-floor distance bending forward; arching back (painful? how far?).
6. 5 × sit-to-stand (seconds) or the 30-second chair stand.
7. 10 m fast walk (seconds); for stenosis, time or distance until symptoms start.
8. Trunk endurance: side-bridge hold time each side (physio-level).
9. Nerve check if any leg symptoms: heel and toe walking, SLR angle.
MEANINGFUL CHANGE: about 30% improvement from baseline on pain or disability scores (Ostelo 2008).

2. Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS): the patient names their 3 hardest tasks and rates each 0–10 — this becomes the goal list. Prompt with local tasks: floor sitting and rising, squatting toilet, bending to sweep or wash clothes, carrying water or head-loads, field work, riding a two-wheeler, lifting a child.
3. Disability questionnaire: Roland-Morris (24 items) or the Oswestry Disability Index — check for a validated Hindi or Marathi version.
4. Body chart: where the symptoms reach — watch for centralisation across visits.
5. Movement: fingertip-to-floor distance bending forward; arching back (painful? how far?).
6. 5 × sit-to-stand (seconds) or the 30-second chair stand.
7. 10 m fast walk (seconds); for stenosis, time or distance until symptoms start.
8. Trunk endurance: side-bridge hold time each side (physio-level).
9. Nerve check if any leg symptoms: heel and toe walking, SLR angle.
fields.MEANINGFUL CHANGE: about 30% improvement from baseline on pain or disability scores (Ostelo 2008).

spine:LS4-4.title: LS4-4 · ADD-ON MODULE — pick the one that matches the working diagnosis
spine:LS4-4.sourceText:

Sciatica module (LD6, LD7): leg pain 0–10 apart from back pain; SLR angle; nerve screen at every visit (any new weakness → L5).
Stenosis module (LD8): walking time or distance to symptom onset and maximum; Zurich Claudication Questionnaire; Timed Up-and-Go; Romberg.
Pelvic girdle module (LD10): Pelvic Girdle Questionnaire; active straight-leg raise score 0–10.
Yellow-flag module (LD5, LD11, or STarT Back HIGH): STarT Back; Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire or Tampa Scale; PHQ-9 mood screen → doctor if moderate or worse; sleep.
Bone-health module (LD12): height to the millimetre at each visit; back-of-head-to-wall distance; Timed Up-and-Go; falls in the last year.

spine:n1_6839.title: PAIN RULES FOR HOME EXERCISE
spine:n1_6839.sourceText:
PAIN RULES FOR HOME EXERCISE
• Pain up to about 5 out of 10 during exercise is acceptable if it has settled back to its usual level by the next morning. If not, hold or step down one level.
• Centralisation rule: symptoms moving toward the spine = good; spreading further down the leg = stop that exercise.
• Any new numbness, weakness, or bladder or bowel change → stop and re-run Stage 1.

LEVEL UP

Re-run the Stage 1 safety screen; re-test directional preference (LT1); re-score STarT Back and yellow flags; physio video exam; doctor review if leg symptoms aren’t improving by 6–8 weeks.

spine:G-NK.title: NECK & UPPER BACK PATHWAY
spine:G-NK.sourceText:
NECK & UPPER BACK PATHWAY
Stage 1 safety screen (12 checks) → Stage 2 which neck or upper-back problem is it (12 working diagnoses) → Stage 3 exercise group (6 groups + a core programme) → Stage 4 measure, dose, re-test.

spine:NS1.title: STAGE 1 — SAFETY SCREEN: Is this neck or upper-back pain safe to treat with exercise?
spine:NS1.sourceText:
STAGE 1 — SAFETY SCREEN: Is this neck or upper-back pain safe to treat with exercise?
Ask the 12 checks in order, most time-critical first. Any YES stops the pathway and names the action. All NO → Stage 2.
The neck carries the spinal cord and the arteries to the brain, and the upper back sits beside the heart, lungs and aorta — so this screen has more “not from the spine” checks than the low-back one (IFOMPT cervical framework, Rushton 2023; red-flag framework, Finucane 2020).

spine:n1_6991.title: SAFETY MODIFIERS — not stops; they change who signs off and how hard you start
spine:n1_6991.sourceText:
SAFETY MODIFIERS — not stops; they change who signs off and how hard you start
• Chest pain, breathlessness or fainting with effort → doctor before progressive exercise.
• Uncontrolled blood pressure → doctor first; no breath-holding during neck strengthening.
• Rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome or previous neck surgery → no end-range or manipulative neck techniques.
• Osteoporosis → avoid loaded bending of the upper back (Group NX-F).
• After a head knock: headache, dizziness or poor concentration may be concussion → doctor review and a graded return.

YELLOW FLAGS — record now, score in Stage 4
• After whiplash: older age, high early pain and disability, and stress-reaction symptoms (startle, nightmares) predict slow recovery (Ritchie 2013). Worry, low mood, poor sleep and work stress matter as much as posture.

CONTEXT TO RECORD (changes the plan)
• Head-load carrying; long hours at a sewing machine, loom, computer or phone; two-wheeler riding on rough roads; looking down for floor or field work; pillow and sleeping position.

spine:N1.title: N1 · Heart, aorta or lungs disguised as neck or upper-back pain
spine:N1.sourceText:
N1 · Heart, aorta or lungs disguised as neck or upper-back pain
ASK: Pain between the shoulder blades, in the jaw, neck or left arm that comes with effort, sweating, breathlessness, nausea or a racing heart? Sudden, severe, tearing pain going through to the back? Sharp pain on breathing with breathlessness or coughing blood? A recent long journey, surgery or a swollen calf?
CHECK: do neck, shoulder and trunk movements change the pain at all? Pulse, blood pressure (both arms if the pain is tearing), breathing rate.
POSITIVE IF: pain not changed by movement, with any feature above.
NOTE: a heart attack, a tear in the aorta (aortic dissection) or a clot in the lung can show up as upper-back or neck pain alone — especially in women, older adults and people with diabetes (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained; basic kit (BP cuff)
Possible heart, aorta or lung cause?

spine:N1Y.title: EMERGENCY — NOW
spine:N1Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — NOW
Call for emergency transfer. Keep the patient at rest. No exercise.

spine:N2.title: N2 · Neck fracture or ligament injury after trauma — Canadian C-Spine Rule
spine:N2.sourceText:
N2 · Neck fracture or ligament injury after trauma — Canadian C-Spine Rule
ASK: A fall, road accident, diving accident or blow to the head recently?
CHECK — Canadian C-Spine Rule (alert, stable adults):
1. High risk → stop: age 65 or over; a dangerous mechanism (fall from 1 m or 5 stairs, a load landing on the head as in diving, a high-speed or rollover road accident, a bicycle crash); or tingling in the arms or legs.
2. A low-risk factor allows movement testing: simple rear-end car crash; sitting comfortably; walking since the injury; neck pain that came on later; no tenderness on the bony midline.
3. Can they actively turn the head 45° to the left and right?
EVIDENCE: sensitivity 100% (95% CI 98–100%), specificity 42.5% for important neck injury (Stiell 2001). The NEXUS criteria give similar safety (sensitivity 99.6%, Hoffman 2000). A negative rule makes a fracture very unlikely.
WHO: anyone trained
A high-risk factor, OR no low-risk factor, OR can’t turn 45° each way?

EMERGENCY
Keep the head and neck still (hands either side of the head or a collar), lie them flat, emergency transfer for imaging. No neck movement or exercise.

spine:N3.title: N3 · Stroke or torn neck artery (cervical artery dissection, posterior circulation problem)
spine:N3.sourceText:
N3 · Stroke or torn neck artery (cervical artery dissection, posterior circulation problem)
ASK: Sudden severe neck pain or headache unlike any before (“worst ever”), especially after neck trauma, a sudden twist or neck manipulation? Any of the 5 Ds and 3 Ns: Dizziness, Double vision, Difficulty speaking, Difficulty swallowing, Drop attacks (sudden falls without fainting); Nausea, Nystagmus (flickering eyes), Numbness of the face or one side? Unsteady walking? A droopy eyelid with a small pupil?
CHECK: blood pressure; watch the eyes as they follow your finger; finger-to-nose; heel-to-toe walk; face symmetry and speech.
NOTE: positional “artery tests” (holding the neck turned) are NOT reliable and must not be used to clear a patient — the history and neurological signs decide (IFOMPT cervical framework, Rushton 2023).
WHO: anyone trained

spine:N4.title: N4 · Meningitis or other serious infection
spine:N4.sourceText:
N4 · Meningitis or other serious infection
ASK: Fever with a severe headache and a stiff neck? Dislike of bright light, vomiting, confusion, a rash that doesn’t fade when pressed with a glass? In a child: a stiff, painful neck with fever, drooling or difficulty swallowing (throat abscess)? Spinal infection risks as in L3 (injecting drugs, recent spinal procedure, diabetes, weak immunity)?
CHECK: temperature; can they bring the chin to the chest? How alert are they? Look for the rash.
NOTE: neck stiffness and the classic bedside meningitis signs are missing in many real cases — a normal neck does not clear meningitis when the story fits (consensus).
WHO: basic kit (thermometer)
Fever with headache, stiff neck, confusion or rash?

spine:N4Y.sourceText:

spine:N5.title: N5 · Giant cell arteritis or polymyalgia rheumatica (over 50)
spine:N5.sourceText:
N5 · Giant cell arteritis or polymyalgia rheumatica (over 50)
ASK: Over 50 with a NEW headache, a tender scalp or temples, jaw pain when chewing, or any change in vision? OR aching and stiffness of BOTH shoulders and the neck (often the hips too) for more than 45 minutes every morning, with tiredness or weight loss?
CHECK: feel the temples (tender, thickened or pulseless artery); can they lift both arms above the head? Stiffness of both shoulder and hip girdles.
NOTE: giant cell arteritis can cause sudden, permanent blindness — vision change or jaw pain while chewing = same day. Polymyalgia improves dramatically with steroids prescribed by a doctor (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained

spine:N5Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — SAME DAY (headache, jaw or vision)

Girdle stiffness alone (polymyalgia) → URGENT, doctor within days. No exercise programme until treated.

spine:N6.title: N6 · Spinal cord compression in the neck (degenerative cervical myelopathy)
spine:N6.sourceText:
N6 · Spinal cord compression in the neck (degenerative cervical myelopathy)
ASK: Clumsy hands — dropping things, trouble with buttons, writing or a phone? Numb hands on both sides? Unsteady, stiff or wide-based walking, or falls? NEW bladder urgency? Electric shocks down the spine when bending the head forward?
CHECK — Cook cluster (5 findings): (1) gait deviation (wide-based, unsteady, can’t walk heel-to-toe); (2) Hoffmann’s sign — flick the middle fingertip; the thumb and index finger twitch = positive; (3) inverted supinator sign — tap the forearm near the wrist; the fingers bend instead of the elbow; (4) Babinski — stroke the sole; the big toe goes UP; (5) age over 45.
EVIDENCE: none of the 5 positive helps rule myelopathy out (LR− 0.18); 3 or more of 5 rules it in (LR+ 30.9) (Cook 2010).
WHO: anyone trained (history, gait); physio-level (reflex signs)
Myelopathy symptoms with 1 or more positive findings — or getting worse?

spine:N6Y.sourceText:
URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
Doctor or spine surgeon, and an MRI. Hands or walking getting worse quickly → same day. No neck manipulation or end-range neck arching. Mild, stable myelopathy may later be offered supervised rehab with close monitoring — only after specialist review (AO Spine guideline, Fehlings 2017).

spine:N7.title: N7 · Unstable upper neck (atlanto-axial instability)
spine:N7.sourceText:
N7 · Unstable upper neck (atlanto-axial instability)
ASK: Rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome, a recent neck injury, or (in a child) a recent throat or ear infection? Does the head feel too heavy — needing the hands to hold it up? A lump-in-the-throat feeling, tingling of the lips or face, or symptoms when bending the head forward?
CHECK: the Sharp-Purser test is physio-level only — sitting, head slightly bent forward; steady the second neck bone and gently glide the head backward. A “clunk” with relief of symptoms = positive. Specificity 96%, positive predictive value 85% in rheumatoid arthritis (Uitvlugt 1988).
WHO: anyone trained (history); physio-level (test)
A risk factor with upper-neck instability symptoms?

spine:N7Y.sourceText:

spine:N8.title: N8 · Fracture without major trauma, cancer, or TB in the neck or upper back
spine:N8.sourceText:
N8 · Fracture without major trauma, cancer, or TB in the neck or upper back
ASK: Past cancer (especially breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid, myeloma)? Unexplained weight loss, night sweats, evening fevers, TB contact? Constant pain worse at night or lying down? Over 50 with first-ever mid-back pain? Steroid tablets or osteoporosis, with sudden pain after a minor strain, cough or lift? Pain wrapping around the chest like a belt?
CHECK: closed-fist percussion down the spine (sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 90% for acute osteoporotic fracture — Langdon 2010); look for a sharp angled hump (gibbus); weigh; check leg strength and walking — cord pressure from the upper back shows up in the LEGS.
NOTE: the thoracic (mid) spine is the commonest site of spinal cancer spread and of spinal TB; persistent mid-back pain is itself a warning sign (consensus; Finucane 2020).

spine:N9.sourceText:
N9 · Shingles (herpes zoster) — a band of burning pain

NOTE: the pain often starts 2–3 days BEFORE the rash. Early antiviral treatment (ideally within about 72 hours of the rash) reduces complications (consensus).

spine:N9Y.sourceText:

Doctor promptly for antiviral treatment and pain control; a rash near the eye = same day. Not an exercise problem — gentle movement is fine.

spine:N10.title: N10 · Child or teenager with neck or upper-back pain
spine:N10.sourceText:
N10 · Child or teenager with neck or upper-back pain
ASK: Under 18? A sudden wry neck with fever, sore throat, or after a throat or ear infection? A head tilt with headache, vomiting or clumsiness? A teenager with a rigid, painful hump of the upper back, or a painful, stiff curve (scoliosis)? Night pain?
CHECK: forward-bend test from the side and from behind: a smooth curve that straightens when they arch (posture) vs a sharp, rigid hump that doesn’t; a rib hump; is the curve painful?
NOTE: most teenage scoliosis is painless — a PAINFUL curve needs a doctor to rule out a bone tumour, infection or spinal cord problem. Scheuermann’s disease causes a rigid upper-back hump with mid-back pain in teens; X-ray confirms it (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained

spine:N10Y.sourceText:

Doctor for an X-ray. Fever, neurological signs, night pain, or a wry neck with fever → URGENT (days) or the same day.

spine:N11.title: N11 · Inflammatory spinal disease (axial spondyloarthritis) or rheumatoid neck
spine:N11.sourceText:
N11 · Inflammatory spinal disease (axial spondyloarthritis) or rheumatoid neck
ASK: Neck or upper-back stiffness for more than 30 minutes every morning that eases with movement? Back pain that began before 40 and improves with exercise, not rest (the ASAS 5 — see L10)? Pain or stiffness on taking a deep breath? Known rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, bowel disease, a red painful eye? Swollen small joints of the hands?
CHECK: count swollen joints (hands, wrists, feet); chest expansion with a tape measure at nipple level — under about 2.5 cm suggests stiffness of the rib joints (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained; basic kit (tape measure)

spine:N11Y.title: REFER — WITHIN WEEKS
spine:N11Y.sourceText:
REFER — WITHIN WEEKS
Doctor or rheumatologist. Rheumatoid arthritis with neck symptoms → check N7 first. Mobility and posture exercise helps alongside the medicines.

spine:N12.title: N12 · Pain coming from the shoulder (or elsewhere)
spine:N12.sourceText:
N12 · Pain coming from the shoulder (or elsewhere)
ASK: Is the pain mainly at the top or outer side of the upper arm? Worse lifting the arm, lying on that side, or reaching behind the back?
CHECK: turn and tip the head — does it reproduce the familiar pain? Then lift the arm forward and out to the side, and rotate the shoulder — does that?
POSITIVE IF: shoulder movement reproduces it; neck movement doesn’t.
NOTE: pain over the top of the shoulder spreading toward the elbow often comes from the neck; pain at the outer upper arm that worsens with arm movement usually comes from the shoulder. Both can coexist. Right shoulder-blade pain after fatty meals → gallbladder (treat like N1: doctor) (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained
Is the shoulder the source?

SWITCH PATHWAY
Shoulder assessment (separate pathway). If BOTH neck and shoulder movements reproduce it, assess and treat both.

spine:NPASS.sourceText:
ALL 12 = NO → EXERCISE-RESPONSIVE (BY EXCLUSION)
Go to Stage 2. Safety-net advice for everyone: come back at once with new dizziness, double vision, speech or swallowing trouble, clumsy hands or unsteady walking. Confirmed by improvement at the week-4 re-test.

spine:NS2.title: STAGE 2 — WHICH NECK OR UPPER-BACK PROBLEM IS IT?
spine:NS2.sourceText:
STAGE 2 — WHICH NECK OR UPPER-BACK PROBLEM IS IT?
The JOSPT neck pain guideline (Blanpied 2017) sorts neck pain into 4 patterns that each need a different emphasis: mobility deficits, movement-coordination problems (including whiplash), headache from the neck, and radiating arm pain. This stage adds the upper back (thoracic spine and ribs) and widespread pain, then hands each working diagnosis to an exercise group.

spine:NQ1.title: NQ1 · Where do the symptoms go? (use the body chart from Q0)

NQ1 · Where do the symptoms go? (use the body chart from Q0)
ASK: “Show me everywhere you feel it. Does it go into the arm or the head? Any pins and needles or numbness?”

NQ2 · How did it start?
ASK: “What happened on the first day? Was there an accident or a jolt?”

Woke up with it — neck stuck to one side, sudden, no injury

spine:NT1.title: NT1 · Whiplash grading (Quebec Task Force) and recovery risk
spine:NT1.sourceText:
NT1 · Whiplash grading (Quebec Task Force) and recovery risk
GRADE (Spitzer 1995): 0 — no neck complaint; I — neck pain or stiffness only, no signs; II — plus reduced movement and tender points; III — plus neurological signs (weakness, reflex or sensory loss) → also run the arm-nerve check (NT3); IV — fracture or dislocation (should already have been caught at N2).
RECOVERY RISK (Ritchie 2013 prediction rule): older age, high early disability on the Neck Disability Index and stress-reaction (hyperarousal) symptoms predict chronic moderate-to-severe disability; younger people with low early disability are likely to recover fully.
ALSO ASK: headache, dizziness or poor concentration after a head knock → doctor for a concussion check.
WHO: anyone trained

spine:ND3.title: ND3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Whiplash-associated disorder (grade I–II), low risk — neck pain with movement-coordination impairment
spine:ND3.sourceText:
ND3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Whiplash-associated disorder (grade I–II), low risk — neck pain with movement-coordination impairment
WHAT IT IS: sprain-type neck pain after a sudden acceleration–deceleration; most people recover within weeks to a few months.
NEXT STEP: reassurance and advice to stay active and keep the neck moving; early active range-of-motion exercise; then deep-neck-flexor, shoulder-blade and endurance training. Education plus active exercise is the recommended first-line care (JOSPT 2017).
AVOID: soft collars and rest; repeated passive treatments.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-B (early mobility) → NX-A (deep neck & shoulder-blade control)
STAGE 4 MODULE: whiplash module.

spine:ND4.title: ND4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Whiplash-associated disorder — HIGH risk of persistent pain
spine:ND4.sourceText:
ND4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Whiplash-associated disorder — HIGH risk of persistent pain
WHAT IT IS: whiplash with high early pain and disability, stress-reaction symptoms or widespread sensitivity — a pattern linked with slow recovery.
NEXT STEP: the same active approach delivered as psychologically informed care: education about pain and stress, graded activity, pacing and sleep; screen for post-traumatic stress and low mood and involve a counsellor or doctor; follow up closely in the first 3 months. In established chronic whiplash, a comprehensive 12-session exercise programme was no better than simple advice (Michaleff 2014, PROMISE trial) — so keep it simple, active and confidence-building rather than intensive.
AVOID: collars, rest, frequent passive treatment, alarming explanations.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-E (graded activity) + NX-A
STAGE 4 MODULE: whiplash module + yellow-flag module.

spine:ND5.title: ND5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Acute wry neck (acute torticollis, adult)
spine:ND5.sourceText:
ND5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Acute wry neck (acute torticollis, adult)
WHAT IT IS: sudden painful locking of the neck, often on waking, turned or tilted to one side, with no injury and no neurological signs. Usually settles over days to a week or two (consensus).
NEXT STEP: reassurance; heat; gentle active movement in the pain-free direction first, then easing into the stiff direction; keep usual activities. A physio may add gentle mobilisation.
AVOID: forcing the neck into the painful direction; collars.
CHECK: a CHILD with a wry neck, fever or neurological signs belongs at N4 / N10, not here.
EXERCISE GROUP: NX-B (mobility)
STAGE 4 MODULE: neck module.

spine:NT2.title: NT2 · Neck movement and endurance check
spine:NT2.sourceText:
NT2 · Neck movement and endurance check
• Active range: turn left and right, tip each ear to the shoulder, look up and down (phone inclinometer app if available). Note which movements are limited and painful at the end of range.
• Upper-back stiffness: sitting with hands behind the head, twist and arch; lying face down, gentle pressure on each thoracic vertebra (physio-level) — stiff, sore levels?
• Deep neck flexor endurance: lying on the back, tuck the chin (a gentle nod) and lift the head 2–3 cm; time the hold until the chin pokes forward or the head drops. Record the seconds as a baseline (consensus).
• Load pattern: do sustained desk, sewing or phone postures, or repetitive arm work, reproduce the pain more than single neck movements?
WHO: anyone trained; physio-level (segmental pressure)

spine:ND1.title: ND1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Neck pain with mobility deficits (mechanical neck pain)
spine:ND1.sourceText:
ND1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Neck pain with mobility deficits (mechanical neck pain)
WHAT IT IS: central or one-sided neck pain with limited, painful end-range movement and stiff neck or upper-back segments; may refer to the shoulder blade or upper arm (not below the elbow).
NEXT STEP: neck range-of-motion exercise, upper-back (thoracic) mobility, shoulder-blade strengthening and deep-neck-flexor work. A physio may add thoracic manipulation and neck mobilisation, which the JOSPT guideline supports alongside exercise (Blanpied 2017).
AVOID: prolonged rest, collars.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-B (mobility) → NX-C (strength & endurance)
STAGE 4 MODULE: neck module.

spine:ND2.title: ND2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Neck pain with movement-coordination / endurance impairment (posture- and load-related neck pain)
spine:ND2.sourceText:
ND2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Neck pain with movement-coordination / endurance impairment (posture- and load-related neck pain)
WHAT IT IS: neck and upper-shoulder (trapezius) pain that builds with sustained postures — sewing, desk or phone work, driving — or repetitive arm work, with poor endurance of the deep neck and shoulder-blade muscles. The posture is not “wrong”; the tissues are under-prepared for the hours spent in it.
NEXT STEP: specific neck–shoulder strengthening — in women office workers with chronic neck muscle pain, 10 weeks of shoulder strength training cut the worst neck pain by about 79% (Andersen 2008) — plus deep-neck-flexor endurance, postural variety and a short movement break every 30–45 minutes.
AVOID: “posture correction” or long static stretching on their own.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-C (strength & endurance) + NX-A
STAGE 4 MODULE: neck module.
