spine:NT3.title: NT3 · Arm nerve-root check (cervical radiculopathy) — Wainner cluster
spine:NT3.sourceText:
NT3 · Arm nerve-root check (cervical radiculopathy) — Wainner cluster
• Upper limb tension test A (median nerve): lying on the back; hold the shoulder blade down, take the arm out to the side palm up, extend the wrist and fingers, slowly straighten the elbow, then tip the head away. Reproduces the arm symptoms = positive. A NEGATIVE test is the most useful single finding for ruling radiculopathy out (Wainner 2003).
• Spurling’s test: head tipped toward the painful side with gentle downward pressure — reproduces the arm pain.
• Distraction test: gently lifting the head (taking its weight) eases the arm pain.
• Rotation under 60° toward the painful side.
CLUSTER: all 4 positive → LR+ 30.3 (Wainner 2003); 3 of 4 → likely.
• Shoulder abduction relief sign: resting the hand on top of the head eases the arm pain — supports a nerve-root cause.
• Neurological screen (compare sides): C5 — lift the arm sideways, biceps reflex; C6 — bend the elbow, extend the wrist, thumb feeling; C7 — straighten the elbow, triceps reflex, middle-finger feeling; C8 — grip, little-finger feeling; T1 — spread the fingers.
WHO: physio-level (tests, reflexes); anyone trained (history, hand-on-head sign)

spine:ND7.title: ND7 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve root in the neck)
spine:ND7.sourceText:
ND7 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve root in the neck)
WHAT IT IS: an irritated nerve root (from a disc bulge or bony narrowing) causing arm pain, usually below the elbow, with pins and needles, numbness or mild weakness in one root’s area. Most people improve over weeks to months without surgery.
NEXT STEP: positions of ease (hand resting on the head, pillow support); repeated chin tucks if they ease or centralise the arm pain; nerve sliders; deep-neck-flexor and shoulder-blade strengthening. A physio may add intermittent traction combined with exercise and mobilisation, which the JOSPT guideline supports (Blanpied 2017).
AVOID: sustained looking up or tipping the head toward the painful side; nerve stretching; heavy overhead lifting while it is acute.
REFER IF: worsening weakness, symptoms in both arms (N6), or severe pain not improving by 6–12 weeks.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-D (nerve-friendly) + NX-A
STAGE 4 MODULE: arm-pain module.

spine:ND8.title: ND8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Suspected neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
spine:ND8.sourceText:
ND8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Suspected neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
WHAT IT IS: irritation of the arm nerves (brachial plexus) between the collarbone, first rib and neck muscles: tingling, heaviness or aching down the inner arm to the ring and little fingers, worse with arms overhead or carrying heavy bags or head-loads. No bedside test is accurate — it is a pattern diagnosis after the neck and wrist have been checked (consensus).
CHECK ALSO: night tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, shaken off on waking → carpal tunnel syndrome at the wrist (not this pathway).
NEXT STEP: shoulder-blade elevation and retraction strength, posture variety, relaxed belly breathing, nerve sliders, load management (bag weight, strap position, head-load technique).
REFER IF: hand swelling, colour change or coldness (blood-vessel type — urgent), or wasting of the small hand muscles.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-D (nerve-friendly) + NX-C
STAGE 4 MODULE: arm-pain module.

spine:NT4.title: NT4 · Headache-from-the-neck check (cervicogenic headache)
spine:NT4.sourceText:
NT4 · Headache-from-the-neck check (cervicogenic headache)
FIRST: any new, sudden, “worst ever”, steadily worsening, morning-vomiting or neurological headache → back to N3 / N4 / N5.
FEATURES (ICHD-3): one-sided headache that starts in the neck and spreads forward; brought on by neck movement or sustained neck postures; reduced neck movement; pressing on the upper neck reproduces the headache.
CHECK — cervical flexion-rotation test: lying on the back, bend the neck fully forward, then turn the head each way. Rotation limited by about 10° or more compared with the other side = positive. Sensitivity 91%, specificity 90% for C1–2 cervicogenic headache in experienced hands (Ogince 2007).
ALSO SCREEN: migraine (throbbing, nausea, light sensitivity, aura) and tension-type headache (both sides, band-like pressure) — these need a different plan.
WHO: physio-level (flexion-rotation test); anyone trained (history)

spine:ND9.title: ND9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Cervicogenic headache (neck pain with headache)
spine:ND9.sourceText:
ND9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Cervicogenic headache (neck pain with headache)
WHAT IT IS: headache referred from the upper neck joints (C1–C3) and muscles: one-sided, starting in the neck, brought on by neck postures or movement.
NEXT STEP: craniocervical flexion training (deep neck flexors), shoulder-blade muscle training and posture variety, plus neck mobility; a physio may add upper-neck mobilisation or manipulation. In a 12-month trial, specific exercise and manipulative therapy each reduced headache frequency and intensity, and the effects lasted (Jull 2002).
AVOID: long static postures without breaks; daily painkillers (risk of medication-overuse headache).
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-A (deep neck & shoulder-blade control) + NX-B
STAGE 4 MODULE: headache module.

spine:NX1.sourceText:
HEADACHE NOT FROM THE NECK
Doctor for headache diagnosis and medicines. Regular aerobic exercise and neck–shoulder strengthening can still help alongside for migraine and tension-type headache (consensus); use Group NX-C or NX-E if neck pain coexists.

spine:NQ3.title: NQ3 · What brings on the upper-back pain?
spine:NQ3.sourceText:
NQ3 · What brings on the upper-back pain?
ASK: “What makes it worse — breathing, coughing, twisting, sitting, lifting the arms?”

spine:NT5.title: NT5 · Rib (costovertebral) joint check
spine:NT5.sourceText:
NT5 · Rib (costovertebral) joint check
• Press along the rib where it meets the spine, and along the rib itself: one tender spot that reproduces the familiar pain?
• Do a deep breath, a cough, side-bending away and trunk rotation reproduce it?
• Spring the rib gently (physio-level).
• Re-check N1 and N9 first: chest pain with effort or breathlessness, or a burning band with skin sensitivity, is NOT a rib-joint problem.
WHO: anyone trained; physio-level (rib springing)

Not reproduced locally → thoracic mobility deficit (ND6)

spine:ND10.title: ND10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Rib (costovertebral) joint pain
spine:ND10.sourceText:
ND10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Rib (costovertebral) joint pain
WHAT IT IS: a sprained or irritated joint where a rib meets the spine — sharp, one-sided pain with breathing, coughing, twisting or rolling in bed, often after lifting, a twist or a bout of coughing. Usually settles over weeks (consensus).
NEXT STEP: breathing exercise (slow deep breaths, expanding the sore side into a hand placed on the ribs), gentle rotation and side-bending mobility, then trunk and shoulder-blade strength.
AVOID: heavy one-sided lifting and twisting while it is irritable.
DANGER: fever, breathlessness, or chest pain with effort → N1.
EXERCISE GROUP: NX-B (mobility — breathing branch)
STAGE 4 MODULE: upper-back module.

spine:ND6.title: ND6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Thoracic (mid / upper-back) pain with mobility deficits
spine:ND6.sourceText:
ND6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Thoracic (mid / upper-back) pain with mobility deficits
WHAT IT IS: aching, stiffness and local pain between or below the shoulder blades, linked with long sitting or bent postures, with stiff, tender thoracic segments and no Stage 1 warning signs.
NEXT STEP: thoracic extension and rotation mobility, shoulder-blade strengthening, breathing and posture variety; a physio may add thoracic mobilisation or manipulation.
AVOID: long slumped postures without breaks.
EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-B (mobility) + NX-C
STAGE 4 MODULE: upper-back module.

spine:ND11.title: ND11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Stooped upper back — age-related hyperkyphosis, or a stable osteoporotic fracture or Scheuermann’s after clearance (from N8 / N10)
spine:ND11.sourceText:
ND11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Stooped upper back — age-related hyperkyphosis, or a stable osteoporotic fracture or Scheuermann’s after clearance (from N8 / N10)
WHAT IT IS: a rounded upper back with weak back-extensor muscles, with or without a healed compression fracture confirmed by the doctor, or teenage Scheuermann’s kyphosis confirmed on X-ray.
NEXT STEP: spinal-extensor strengthening, posture training, chest-opening mobility, balance and fall prevention. In adults over 60 with hyperkyphosis, 6 months of spine-strengthening and posture training reduced the kyphosis angle compared with health education (Katzman 2017); back-extensor exercise was linked with fewer vertebral fractures (Sinaki 2002).
AVOID: loaded bending and twisting of the spine (sit-ups, toe touches).
EXERCISE GROUP: NX-F (spinal extensor & bone-safe strength)
STAGE 4 MODULE: bone-health module.

spine:NT6.title: NT6 · Widespread pain / central sensitisation check
spine:NT6.sourceText:
NT6 · Widespread pain / central sensitisation check
• Clinical criteria (all 3): pain out of proportion to the injury or findings; pain spread widely or not following anatomy; over-sensitive to touch, pressure, cold, light, sound or stress (Nijs 2015).
• Central Sensitization Inventory: 40 or more out of 100 suggests central sensitisation (sensitivity 81%, specificity 75%; Neblett 2013).
• After whiplash, widespread sensitivity and stress symptoms often travel together — check NT1 risk features.
• Re-check N5 (polymyalgia) and N11 (inflammatory disease) in older or morning-stiff patients.
WHO: anyone trained (questions); physio-level (interpretation)

spine:ND12.title: ND12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic neck pain with widespread pain / central sensitisation (nociplastic pain)
spine:ND12.sourceText:
ND12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic neck pain with widespread pain / central sensitisation (nociplastic pain)
WHAT IT IS: a sensitised nervous system: neck pain plus pain in many areas, flaring easily and out of proportion to any tissue problem; often with poor sleep, fatigue and stress. Real pain — not imagined, and not damage.
NEXT STEP: pain education first; graded activity and graded exposure to avoided tasks (driving, overhead work, looking up); regular aerobic exercise starting low and building slowly; gentle neck–shoulder strength; sleep and stress strategies; psychological support (CBT-based) where available.
AVOID: repeated scans, collars, long rest after flares, passive-only care, opioids.
EXERCISE GROUP: NX-E (graded activity & pain education)
STAGE 4 MODULE: yellow-flag module.

spine:n1_6999.title: WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T)
spine:n1_6999.sourceText:
WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T)
Most neck pain has no single tissue cause you can prove without imaging — and scans often show “wear” in people with no pain. What changes care is the pattern: stiff vs poorly controlled, arm-nerve involvement, headache, whiplash recovery risk, and how widespread and sensitised the pain is. So Stage 2 picks the exercise group, the positions to favour and avoid, and the starting dose.
Posture: no single “correct” posture prevents neck pain. Teach variety and breaks, and build the capacity of the tissues for the hours the patient actually spends in that position.

spine:n1_7199.title: STAGE 3 — EXERCISE GROUPS: diagnoses that share a problem share a programme
spine:n1_7199.sourceText:
STAGE 3 — EXERCISE GROUPS: diagnoses that share a problem share a programme
Each working diagnosis points (grey curved arrows) to one or two groups. A group = the shared mechanism + the exercises that target it + how to progress. Pick 3–5 exercises from the group, set the dose in Stage 4, and finish in the CORE PROGRAMME.
Why groups work: the neck pain guideline recommends combining mobility, deep-neck-flexor and shoulder-blade training, strength and endurance in most patterns (Blanpied 2017); the emphasis changes with the pattern, not the whole programme.

spine:NX-A.title: NX-A · Deep neck flexor & shoulder-blade control
spine:NX-A.sourceText:
NX-A · Deep neck flexor & shoulder-blade control
For: ND9 cervicogenic headache · ND3 whiplash (after early mobility) · ND4 high-risk whiplash · ND2 posture- and load-related pain · ND7 radiculopathy (once settled)
SHARED PROBLEM: the deep stabilising muscles at the front of the neck and around the shoulder blade switch on late and tire early, so bigger muscles overwork and the upper neck is overloaded.
• Chin nod (craniocervical flexion) lying on the back, head on a folded towel: a gentle “yes” nod without lifting the head — 10 × 10 s
• Progress with a folded blood-pressure cuff under the neck (pressure biofeedback: 20 → 30 mmHg in 2 mmHg steps) if available
• Chin nod, then lift the head 2–3 cm and hold 5–10 s
• Sitting: chin nod plus gentle hand resistance in each direction (isometrics), 5 × 5–10 s
• Shoulder-blade setting — draw the shoulder blades gently back and down, 10 × 10 s → face-down “Y” and “T” arm lifts
DOSE: daily, 10–15 minutes; quality over load.
EVIDENCE: craniocervical flexion training reduced cervicogenic headache frequency and intensity over 12 months (Jull 2002).

spine:NX-B.title: NX-B · Neck & upper-back mobility (move early)
spine:NX-B.sourceText:
NX-B · Neck & upper-back mobility (move early)
For: ND1 mobility deficits · ND5 acute wry neck · ND3 whiplash (early) · ND6 thoracic mobility deficit · ND10 rib joint pain (breathing branch) · ND9 headache (alongside NX-A)
SHARED PROBLEM: painful, stiff segments — movement in comfortable ranges calms the pain and restores motion.
• Neck turns, tips and nods within comfort: 10 each way, several times a day
• Chin tucks (retraction) sitting tall: 10 reps
• Thoracic extension over a chair back or a rolled towel: 10 reps
• “Open book” rotation lying on the side: 10 each side
• Cat–camel on hands and knees; shoulder rolls; shoulder-blade squeezes
• Breathing branch (ND10): hand on the sore ribs, 5–10 slow deep breaths expanding into the hand, every hour
DOSE: little and often — every 1–2 hours while acute; then 2–3 times a day.
PROGRESS: to NX-A or NX-C within 1–2 weeks.

spine:NX-D.title: NX-D · Nerve-friendly arm-pain care
spine:NX-D.sourceText:
NX-D · Nerve-friendly arm-pain care
For: ND7 cervical radiculopathy · ND8 thoracic outlet syndrome · whiplash with arm symptoms (NT1 grade III)
SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitive nerve in the neck or shoulder girdle that dislikes being squeezed or stretched.
• Positions of ease: hand resting on the head; a pillow under the arm; neck supported in bed
• Chin tucks: 10 reps every 2–3 hours, if they ease or centralise the arm pain
• Median nerve slider: arm out to the side, palm up; bend the wrist back while tipping the head TOWARD that arm, then release both — 10–15 reps, no stretch pain
• Ulnar nerve slider (ND8): make an “OK” sign and bring it gently toward the eye like goggles, 10 reps
• Shoulder-blade elevation and retraction; relaxed belly breathing (ND8)
• Then progress to NX-A and NX-C
RULE: pins and needles or numbness spreading = too much — stop and step down.
EVIDENCE: neural mobilisation reduced pain in chronic neck–arm pain (about 1.9 points out of 10; Basson 2017); traction combined with exercise is supported for radiculopathy (Blanpied 2017).

spine:NX-C.title: NX-C · Neck–shoulder strength & endurance
spine:NX-C.sourceText:
NX-C · Neck–shoulder strength & endurance
For: ND2 posture- and load-related neck pain · ND1 mobility deficits (once movement returns) · ND6 thoracic pain · ND8 thoracic outlet (shoulder-blade elevation branch)
SHARED PROBLEM: neck and shoulder tissues under-prepared for long hours of static work or repetitive arm use.
• Shoulder shrugs holding water bottles or a bag: 3 × 10–12
• Rows with a band, or a towel around a pole: 3 × 10–12
• Reverse fly / band pull-aparts: 3 × 12
• Side raises to shoulder height: 3 × 10
• Wall push-ups → push-up plus (push the shoulder blades apart at the top)
• Neck isometrics — hand resistance forward, back and to each side: 5 × 10 s
• Work breaks: every 30–45 minutes, 1 minute of movement
DOSE: 3 times a week, about 20 minutes; increase the load when the reps get easy (Andersen 2008 ran 10 weeks).
EVIDENCE: specific strength training reduced worst neck pain by about 79% in office workers with chronic neck muscle pain (Andersen 2008).

spine:NX-E.title: NX-E · Graded activity & pain education
spine:NX-E.sourceText:
NX-E · Graded activity & pain education
For: ND12 widespread pain / central sensitisation · ND4 high-risk whiplash · anyone with a high Örebro score
SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitised system, stress and fear of movement — the aim is confidence and capacity.
• Pain education: hurt ≠ harm; whiplash and neck pain are not signs of damage; flare-ups settle
• Walking or cycling programme: start below today’s comfortable amount, add about 10% a week (by plan, not by pain)
• Graded exposure to avoided tasks: driving and shoulder checks, looking up, overhead reaching, carrying
• Gentle whole-body strength: sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, rows, carries
• Relaxed breathing, a sleep routine, pacing between busy and quiet days
DOSE: build toward 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus 2 strength days (WHO 2020).
EVIDENCE: in chronic whiplash, simple advice did as well as a comprehensive exercise programme (Michaleff 2014) — keep the programme simple, active and confidence-building.

spine:NX-F.title: NX-F · Spinal extensor & bone-safe strength (upper back)
spine:NX-F.sourceText:
NX-F · Spinal extensor & bone-safe strength (upper back)
For: ND11 stooped upper back — hyperkyphosis, stable osteoporotic fracture, or Scheuermann’s after clearance
SHARED PROBLEM: weak back extensors and a rounded upper back, often with fragile bones — the goals are extensor strength, alignment and fewer falls.
• Face-down head-and-chest lifts with a pillow under the tummy: 8–10 reps, hold 3 s
• Seated or standing back extension against a wall or chair back: 10 reps
• Wall angels; chin tuck with the back of the head toward the wall: 5 × 10 s
• Rows and reverse flies with a band
• Chest opener: lie on a rolled towel along the spine, arms out, 2–3 min
• Balance and sit-to-stand practice
AVOID: sit-ups, toe touches, loaded twisting.
EVIDENCE: 6 months of spine strengthening and posture training reduced kyphosis in older adults (Katzman 2017); back-extensor strength linked with fewer vertebral fractures (Sinaki 2002); Too Fit To Fracture guidance (Giangregorio 2014).

spine:NX-CORE.title: NX-CORE · CORE PROGRAMME FOR EVERYONE — where every group ends up
spine:NX-CORE.sourceText:
NX-CORE · CORE PROGRAMME FOR EVERYONE — where every group ends up
Once symptoms are settling, every patient moves here.
STRENGTH (2–3 days a week, 2–3 sets of 8–12): rows, push-ups (wall → bench → floor), shoulder presses with light loads, farmer carries, plus sit-to-stand or squats for the whole body.
NECK–SHOULDER ENDURANCE: deep-neck-flexor holds and shoulder-blade work kept up 2–3 times a week.
ENDURANCE: walking, cycling or swimming, building toward 150 minutes a week.
WORK AND LIFE TASKS: practise the patient’s own PSFS goals — head-loads and carrying, sewing or computer sessions with breaks, driving and shoulder checks, sleeping comfortably, looking up to hang washing.
FLARE-UP PLAN: drop back one level for 2–3 days, use the group’s easing movement (chin tucks, gentle turns), keep active, then rebuild.

spine:NS4.title: STAGE 4 — MEASURE, DOSE THE EXERCISE, RE-TEST
spine:NS4.sourceText:
STAGE 4 — MEASURE, DOSE THE EXERCISE, RE-TEST
Every patient comes here from their exercise group. Everyone gets the same short core battery; the diagnosis adds one module; irritability sets the starting dose; the Örebro score sets HOW the programme is delivered.

fields.BODY: Every patient comes here from their exercise group. Everyone gets the same short core battery; the diagnosis adds one module; irritability sets the starting dose; the Örebro score sets HOW the programme is delivered.

spine:NS4-1.title: NS4-1 · How irritable is the neck?
spine:NS4-1.sourceText:
NS4-1 · How irritable is the neck?
ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours, sleep and headaches too.

fields.ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours, sleep and headaches too.

options.label: HIGH: pain at rest or wakes you; small movements flare it; takes hours or until the next day to settle
MODERATE: pain with some activities; settles within an hour or two
LOW: pain only with long or heavy activity; settles within minutes

spine:NS4-HI.title: START GENTLE
spine:NS4-HI.sourceText:
START GENTLE
Positions of ease, NX-B gentle movement, chin nods, short walks, education. Baseline limited to pain, PSFS and the Örebro screen.

fields.BODY: Positions of ease, NX-B gentle movement, chin nods, short walks, education. Baseline limited to pain, PSFS and the Örebro screen.

spine:NS4-MD.title: START MODERATE
spine:NS4-MD.sourceText:
START MODERATE
Group exercises at full dose and progressive strengthening within the pain rules. Full core battery.

fields.BODY: Group exercises at full dose and progressive strengthening within the pain rules. Full core battery.

spine:NS4-LO.title: START STRONGER
spine:NS4-LO.sourceText:
START STRONGER
Core programme loading, carrying and overhead work, return to sport or heavy tasks. Full core battery.

fields.BODY: Core programme loading, carrying and overhead work, return to sport or heavy tasks. Full core battery.

spine:NS4-2.title: NS4-2 · Short-form Örebro Musculoskeletal Pain Screening Questionnaire (10 questions)
spine:NS4-2.sourceText:
NS4-2 · Short-form Örebro Musculoskeletal Pain Screening Questionnaire (10 questions)
Scores the risk of long-term disability from pain, beliefs, mood and work factors across any musculoskeletal pain site. A cut-off of 50 identified 83–85% of the people who went on to develop disability (Linton 2011).
• Lower risk: advice, reassurance, the group’s exercises at home; few contacts.
• Higher risk (50 or more): psychologically informed physiotherapy — tackle fears and beliefs, graded exposure, pacing, goal-setting; involve a counsellor or doctor for low mood or stress-reaction symptoms (especially after whiplash).

spine:NS4-3.title: NS4-3 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes)
spine:NS4-3.sourceText:
NS4-3 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes)
Needs: a chair, a stopwatch, a phone and a tape measure. Repeat the SAME set at week 0, 4 and 12.
1. Pain 0–10 (faces version for low literacy): average and worst in the last week; arm pain and headache scored separately if present.
2. Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS): the patient names their 3 hardest tasks and rates each 0–10 — this becomes the goal list. Prompt with local tasks: carrying head-loads or water, sewing or computer work, looking up to hang washing, driving or riding a two-wheeler, sleeping, floor work.
3. Neck Disability Index (NDI): 10 items, 0–50 — check for a validated Hindi or Marathi version.
4. Body chart: where the symptoms reach — watch arm symptoms centralise across visits.

spine:n1_7275.title: PAIN RULES FOR HOME EXERCISE
spine:n1_7275.sourceText:
PAIN RULES FOR HOME EXERCISE
• Pain up to about 5 out of 10 during exercise is acceptable if it has settled back to its usual level by the next morning. If not, hold or step down one level.
• Arm-symptom rule: symptoms moving up toward the neck = good; spreading down the arm, or new numbness or weakness = stop that exercise and re-check NT3 / N6.
• Dizziness, double vision, or speech or swallowing trouble during exercise → stop at once and go to N3.

hip_knee:HS3-1.title: HS3-1 · How irritable is the hip?
hip_knee:HS3-1.sourceText:

ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets it off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours too.

hip_knee:HS3-2.title: HS3-2 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 12 minutes)
hip_knee:HS3-2.sourceText:
HS3-2 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 12 minutes)
Needs: a chair, a stopwatch, 10 m of floor, a step, a wall and a phone. Repeat the SAME set at week 0, 4 and 12.
1. Pain 0–10 (faces version): average and worst in the last week.
2. Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS): their 3 hardest tasks, each rated 0–10 — this becomes the goal list. Prompt with local tasks: cross-legged floor sitting, rising from the floor, squatting toilet, putting on footwear, climbing into a bus or tractor, field work.
3. 30-second chair stand: count full stands in 30 s, arms crossed.
4. 40 m fast-paced walk: 4 × 10 m, timed.
5. Timed Up-and-Go: rise, walk 3 m, turn, walk back, sit; usual walking aid allowed (walking transitions and falls risk).
6. Hip range of motion: internal rotation with the hip bent 90°, bending, extension — compare sides (phone inclinometer on the shin for rotation).
7. Hip strength in all six directions: handheld dynamometer if available; otherwise side-lying leg-lift hold time and single-leg bridge count.
8. Single-leg stance + Trendelenburg sign: up to 30 s; watch whether the opposite side of the pelvis drops or the trunk leans (weak hip abductors).
9. Gait video: 10 s from the front and side (limp, trunk lean, short stride).
Tests 3–5 come from the OARSI recommended set (Dobson 2013) and the 2025 hip osteoarthritis guideline.

hip_knee:HS2.sourceText:
STAGE 2 — WHICH HIP PROBLEM IS IT?

hip_knee:HD1.title: HD1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Hip osteoarthritis
hip_knee:HD1.sourceText:
HD1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Hip osteoarthritis
WHAT IT IS: “wear and repair” changes in the hip joint; the commonest cause of groin pain in older adults. No X-ray is needed to start care; the guideline keeps X-ray for when the picture is unclear.
NEXT STEP: exercise therapy is the main treatment (strongest recommendation, grade A, JOSPT 2025): individualised strengthening in all directions plus mobility work, typically 1–5 sessions a week for 5–16 weeks; education on pacing and protecting the joint; a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand if it keeps them active; practise their goal tasks (rising from the floor, getting into a vehicle); group programmes such as GLA:D where available (NICE NG226).
AVOID: bracing early in care; passive treatments on their own; weight-loss advice for an underweight patient.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: hip osteoarthritis module.

hip_knee:HT1.title: HT1 · Hip osteoarthritis check (JOSPT hip osteoarthritis guideline, Cibulka 2017; revised 2025)
hip_knee:HT1.sourceText:
HT1 · Hip osteoarthritis check (JOSPT hip osteoarthritis guideline, Cibulka 2017; revised 2025)
Typical: age 50+; moderate groin, front or side hip pain with weight-bearing; morning stiffness under 1 hour; trouble with socks, shoes, cross-legged sitting and squatting.
Key sign — internal rotation (hip and knee bent 90°, swing the foot outward so the hip turns inward): less than 24°, OR internal rotation and bending both 15° less than the other side, and/or pain on passive internal rotation.
Extra confidence — Sutlive cluster (count 5): 1) squatting aggravates; 2) active hip bending causes side-hip pain; 3) the scour test with adduction causes side-hip or groin pain; 4) active hip extension (leg backward) is painful; 5) passive internal rotation 25° or less. 4 of 5 → LR+ 24.3, probability of osteoarthritis about 91% (Sutlive 2008; small study, not yet validated).
ACR clinical criteria: sensitivity 86%, specificity 75% (Altman 1991).
WHO: physio-level (rotation); anyone trained (history)

hip_knee:HD2.title: HD2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Hip-related pain — FAI syndrome, hip dysplasia or labral tear (Zurich consensus, Reiman 2020)
hip_knee:HD2.sourceText:
HD2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Hip-related pain — FAI syndrome, hip dysplasia or labral tear (Zurich consensus, Reiman 2020)
WHAT IT IS: in young and middle-aged active adults: FAI (femoroacetabular impingement — extra bone on the ball or socket pinches during deep bending), dysplasia (a shallow socket), or a tear of the labrum (the cartilage rim of the socket).
CONFIRM: groin pain with long sitting, deep squats, getting in and out of vehicles, or pivoting; clicking or catching; positive FADIR. FADIR catches 96–99% of cases but is also positive in many people without the problem — a NEGATIVE test helps rule it out; a positive test doesn’t confirm it (Reiman 2015). The subtype cannot be known without imaging, and the exercise approach is shared.
NEXT STEP: physio-led care: activity modification + exercise (guideline grade B), movement-pattern training and education (grade C) (JOSPT, Enseki 2023). Hip and trunk strength from isometric to heavy; practise squats, stairs and vehicle transfers.
AVOID EARLY: repeated deep bending with rotation (deep squats, long cross-legged sitting) while irritable — this collides with floor sitting and squatting toilets, so plan around it.
REFER (X-ray, orthopaedic opinion) IF: no progress by about 12 weeks.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: young-hip module.

fields.WHAT IT IS: in young and middle-aged active adults: FAI (femoroacetabular impingement — extra bone on the ball or socket pinches during deep bending), dysplasia (a shallow socket), or a tear of the labrum (the cartilage rim of the socket).
fields.CONFIRM: groin pain with long sitting, deep squats, getting in and out of vehicles, or pivoting; clicking or catching; positive FADIR. FADIR catches 96–99% of cases but is also positive in many people without the problem — a NEGATIVE test helps rule it out; a positive test doesn’t confirm it (Reiman 2015). The subtype cannot be known without imaging, and the exercise approach is shared.

hip_knee:HD3.title: HD3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Adductor-related groin pain
hip_knee:HD3.sourceText:
HD3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Adductor-related groin pain
WHAT IT IS: an overloaded inner-thigh (adductor) tendon where it attaches near the pubic bone; very common in kicking and cutting sports (football, kabaddi, cricket).
CONFIRM (Doha): tender adductor tendon + pain on resisted squeeze.
NEXT STEP: adductor isometrics (squeeze holds), then progressive strengthening such as side-lying and Copenhagen-style adduction; hip and trunk strength; graded return to sprinting, kicking and change of direction.
AVOID: full kicking and sprinting while the squeeze test is painful.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: groin module.

hip_knee:HD4.title: HD4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Iliopsoas-related groin pain
hip_knee:HD4.sourceText:
HD4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Iliopsoas-related groin pain
WHAT IT IS: an overloaded deep hip-flexor muscle (iliopsoas) at the front of the groin, from kicking, sprinting or repeated hip bending.
CONFIRM (Doha): tender iliopsoas + pain on resisted hip bending and/or stretch.
NEXT STEP: hip-flexor isometrics, then progressive strengthening; trunk and hip strength.
AVOID: aggressive hip-flexor stretching while irritable.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: groin module.

hip_knee:HD5.title: HD5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Inguinal-related groin pain
hip_knee:HD5.sourceText:
HD5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Inguinal-related groin pain
WHAT IT IS: pain at the inguinal canal (the passage just above the groin crease), with no hernia.
CONFIRM (Doha): pain and tenderness at the inguinal canal, no palpable hernia, worse with resisted sit-ups, coughing or straining.
NEXT STEP: graded trunk (abdominal) and hip strengthening.
AVOID: heavy straining while painful.
REFER IF: a bulge appears (surgical referral; sometimes an ultrasound is needed to tell the difference).
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: groin module.

hip_knee:HD6.title: HD6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Pubic-related groin pain
hip_knee:HD6.sourceText:
HD6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Pubic-related groin pain
WHAT IT IS: irritation of the pubic joint at the front of the pelvis; sometimes after pregnancy, more often in kicking and running sports.
CONFIRM (Doha): local tenderness of the pubic symphysis and the bone right beside it.
NEXT STEP: graded loading as for adductor-related pain (HD3).
REFER IF: hopping is painful — a bone stress injury needs imaging (H4).
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: groin module.

hip_knee:HT2.title: HT2 · Groin test set for active people (Doha agreement, Weir 2015)
hip_knee:HT2.sourceText:
HT2 · Groin test set for active people (Doha agreement, Weir 2015)
Do each and note which one reproduces their FAMILIAR pain — more than one can be positive:
A) FADIR — hip bent to 90°, moved across the body (adduction) and turned inward (internal rotation).
B) Adductor squeeze — squeeze a fist or ball between the knees; press the inner-thigh tendon near the pubic bone.
C) Hip-flexor tests — resist lifting the knee while seated; stretch the front of the hip lying at the edge of a bed (Thomas test position); press just below the groin crease.
D) Abdominal tests — resisted sit-up and a cough; press over the inguinal canal (just above the groin crease) and feel for a lump.
E) Pubic bone — press directly on the joint at the front midline of the pelvis (pubic symphysis).
WHO: physio-level

hip_knee:HQ2.title: HQ2 · How old, and how active?
hip_knee:HQ2.sourceText:
HQ2 · How old, and how active?
WHY: hip osteoarthritis is the main cause of groin pain in older adults; in younger active adults, the shape of the hip joint and the groin muscles are more likely causes.

hip_knee:HD7.title: HD7 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Gluteal tendinopathy (side-of-hip pain; often called “trochanteric bursitis”)
hip_knee:HD7.sourceText:
HD7 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Gluteal tendinopathy (side-of-hip pain; often called “trochanteric bursitis”)
WHAT IT IS: the tendons of the buttock muscles that attach to the bony point on the side of the hip are overloaded and compressed.
NEXT STEP: education on load + progressive abductor exercise. In the LEAP trial this beat a steroid injection and “wait and see” at 8 weeks, with better overall improvement than injection at 1 year (Mellor 2018).
• Avoid compressing the tendon: no crossing the legs, hanging on one hip, lying on the painful side without a pillow, or very low seats; a pillow between the knees when side-lying.
• Isometric side holds for pain relief → bridges, step-ups, single-leg work.
AVOID: stretches across the side of the hip (they compress the tendon); steroid injection as the first plan; complete rest.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: side-of-hip module.

hip_knee:HT3.title: HT3 · Side-of-hip check (gluteal tendinopathy — Grimaldi 2017, 65 patients compared with MRI)
hip_knee:HT3.sourceText:
HT3 · Side-of-hip check (gluteal tendinopathy — Grimaldi 2017, 65 patients compared with MRI)
1. Press the bony point on the side of the hip (greater trochanter). NOT tender → gluteal tendinopathy is unlikely (palpation sensitivity 80%).
2. Single-leg stance 30 s: side-on to a wall, one fingertip on the wall, stand on the painful leg for up to 30 seconds. Side-hip pain within 30 s → very likely (specificity 100%, LR+ about 12; small study).
3. Physio add-ons: FADER (hip bent, moved across the body and turned OUTWARD) and passive adduction lying on the side — specificity about 87% each.
HISTORY: can’t lie on that side at night; stairs, standing on one leg, crossing the legs and low seats hurt; more common in women from middle age.
WHO: anyone trained (steps 1–2); physio-level (step 3)

hip_knee:HD9.title: HD9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Hamstring strain injury
hip_knee:HD9.sourceText:
HD9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Hamstring strain injury
WHAT IT IS: a tear in the muscle at the back of the thigh, usually from sprinting or over-stretching.
NEXT STEP — staged loading: early pain-free isometrics and walking → progressive strengthening including slow lengthening (eccentric) work, with Nordic-type exercises later → graded running up to sprinting. Return when strength and range are close to the other side (Martin 2022).
AVOID: aggressive stretching early; sprinting before strength and range have recovered.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: hamstring module.

hip_knee:HT4.title: HT4 · Hamstring strain check (JOSPT hamstring guideline, Martin 2022)
hip_knee:HT4.sourceText:
HT4 · Hamstring strain check (JOSPT hamstring guideline, Martin 2022)
• Find the sorest point and how far the tenderness spreads.
• Lying face down, resist knee bending at 90° and at 15° — pain and weakness?
• Active knee extension range: lying, hip held at 90°, straighten the knee; compare sides (used to track recovery).
POSITIVE IF: tender muscle + pain and weakness on resisted testing.
DANGER SIGN: a gap or big bruise at the sitting bone after a slip into the splits → H11.
WHO: physio-level

hip_knee:HD10.title: HD10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy
hip_knee:HD10.sourceText:
HD10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy
WHAT IT IS: the hamstring tendon is irritated where it attaches to the sitting bone.
CONFIRM: pressing the sitting bone (side-lying, hip bent) reproduces the pain; lying with hip and knee bent, straightening the knee hurts at the sitting bone.
NEXT STEP: tendon loading without compression in deep hip bending — isometric bridge holds, then progress from shallow to deeper hip bending; a cushion on hard seats (consensus).
AVOID EARLY: deep hamstring stretches and long sitting on hard surfaces.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: hamstring module.

Manage with lumbopelvic and hip strengthening and graded activity; a pelvic belt short-term for pregnancy-related pain. Don’t label it as hip pain.

hip_knee:HT5.title: HT5 · Sacroiliac joint check (the joint between the base of the spine and the pelvis) — Laslett cluster
hip_knee:HT5.sourceText:
HT5 · Sacroiliac joint check (the joint between the base of the spine and the pelvis) — Laslett cluster
Six pain-provocation tests: distraction, thigh thrust, compression, sacral thrust, and Gaenslen’s test on each side. Count those that reproduce the familiar pain.
EVIDENCE: 3 or more of 6 positive: sensitivity 94%, specificity 78%. If ALL are negative, the sacroiliac joint can be ruled out (Laslett 2005; compared with diagnostic injections).
RUN ONLY AFTER the back screen (H10).
WHO: physio-level

hip_knee:HD11.title: HD11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Deep gluteal syndrome (includes “piriformis syndrome”)
hip_knee:HD11.sourceText:
HD11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Deep gluteal syndrome (includes “piriformis syndrome”)
WHAT IT IS: irritation of the sciatic nerve deep in the buttock.
CONFIRM: tender deep in the buttock; a seated stretch with the hip bent, crossed and turned inward reproduces buttock or sciatica-like pain — AND spine, sacroiliac joint and hamstring have been cleared. A diagnosis of exclusion; low certainty without imaging or nerve studies.
NEXT STEP: cautious hip strengthening (outward rotators, abductors), sitting breaks and a softer seat (consensus).
AVOID: forceful stretches that bring on nerve symptoms.
WATCH: re-test at week 4; worsening nerve signs → doctor.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: hamstring module.

hip_knee:HQ3.title: HQ3 · Buttock or back-of-thigh pain: how did it start, and where exactly?
hip_knee:HQ3.sourceText:
HQ3 · Buttock or back-of-thigh pain: how did it start, and where exactly?
FIRST: the back must already be cleared (H10) — the spine is a common source of buttock pain.
ASK: “Show me the exact spot. What were you doing when it started?”

hip_knee:HD8.title: HD8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Meralgia paresthetica (squeezed skin nerve of the thigh)
hip_knee:HD8.sourceText:
HD8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Meralgia paresthetica (squeezed skin nerve of the thigh)
WHAT IT IS: the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve — a skin-sensation nerve — is pinched where it passes the front of the pelvic bone. Causes: tight belts, tool belts, waist-tied saris or dhotis, pregnancy, weight change, diabetes.
CONFIRM: a patch of burning, tingling or numbness on the outer-front thigh, with NORMAL strength (light-touch map compared with the other side).
NEXT STEP: loosen belts and waistbands; explain it is a nerve, not the joint. Not an exercise condition (consensus).
REFER IF: any weakness, or it spreads → back problem (H10) or doctor.

WATCH: a hand cupped around the side of the hip (the “C-sign”) usually means pain from deep inside the hip joint, even though the hand is on the side.

“Hip pain” can come from the joint, the tendons around it, the spine, the pelvis or the abdomen. Ask the 12 checks in order, most time-critical first. Any YES stops the pathway and names the action. All NO → Stage 2.

hip_knee:H1.title: H1 · Possible hip fracture
hip_knee:H1.sourceText:
H1 · Possible hip fracture
ASK: Did you fall or hurt the hip? Can you stand and walk on it? Older adult, thin bones (osteoporosis), long-term steroid use?
CHECK:
• Lying on the back, compare the legs — is the painful leg shorter and turned outward?
• Lift the straight leg (active straight-leg raise); gently roll the straight leg in and out (log roll) — groin pain?
• Patellar-pubic percussion: stethoscope on the pubic bone; tap each kneecap in turn and compare the sound — duller on the painful side = positive. For fractures hidden on the first X-ray: sensitivity 96%, specificity 86% (Tiru 2002, as reported in a 2013 review); a later study found 85% / 70%.
NOTE: a patient who can walk can still have a non-displaced fracture.
WHO: anyone trained; basic kit (stethoscope)

hip_knee:H1Y.sourceText:

hip_knee:H2.title: H2 · Hot, irritable hip — possible joint infection
hip_knee:H2.sourceText:
H2 · Hot, irritable hip — possible joint infection
ASK: Fever, chills, feeling unwell? Can you put weight on it? Does ANY movement hurt? Recent infection, injection, diabetes or a weak immune system?
CHECK: temperature; how they hold the leg at rest; very gently roll the leg.
POSITIVE IF: fever; leg held bent and turned out; any rotation is very painful; won’t bear weight.
EVIDENCE (children): Kocher criteria — refuses to bear weight, fever above 38.5 °C, raised ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and white cell count on blood tests. With 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 present, the chance of infection is 0.2% / 3% / 40% / 93% / 99.6% (Kocher 1999). Without blood tests, fever + refusing to bear weight already scores 2 of 4.
ADULTS: treat as infected until proven otherwise; fever is absent in about 4 in 10 (Margaretten 2007). A psoas abscess (pus in the deep hip-flexor muscle; fever, hip held bent, TB risk) looks similar.
WHO: basic kit (thermometer)
Any sign present?

hip_knee:H3.title: H3 · Child or teenager with a limp
hip_knee:H3.sourceText:
H3 · Child or teenager with a limp
ASK: How old? How long has the limp been there? Fever (→ H2)? Overweight, or in a growth spurt? Pain in the groin, thigh OR knee?
CHECK:
• Drehmann sign: lying down, bend the hip to 90° — does the leg swing outward by itself?
• Internal rotation: hip and knee bent 90°, swing the foot outward so the hip turns inward; compare sides — clearly limited or painful?
RULE: an older child or teenager with a limp and limited inward rotation = slipped capital femoral epiphysis (the ball of the hip slipping at the growth plate) until an X-ray says otherwise — about 15% present with knee or thigh pain only (Peck 2017). A younger child with a limp: Perthes disease (loss of blood supply to the ball of the hip) is possible. A toddler, or any fever: go to H2.
WHO: physio-level (hip rotation); anyone trained (history)

hip_knee:H4.title: H4 · Stress fracture of the hip (femoral neck)
hip_knee:H4.sourceText:
H4 · Stress fracture of the hip (femoral neck)
ASK: A recent jump in running, marching, walking distance or heavy labour? Deep groin or thigh pain with weight-bearing that comes on earlier each session — now even when walking? For women: missed periods or low food intake? A past stress fracture?
CHECK:
• Single-leg hop on the painful leg — sharp groin pain? (stop at the first hop that hurts)
• Fulcrum test: seated; the examiner’s forearm under the middle of the thigh as a lever; press down on the knee — sharp pain or apprehension. Sensitivity 88–93%, specificity 13–75% (small studies, secondary source).
• Patellar-pubic percussion as in H1.
NOTE: suspicion alone is enough to stop impact loading. Early X-rays are often normal, and fractures on the upper side of the femoral neck can displace.
WHO: physio-level; anyone trained (history)

hip_knee:H5.title: H5 · Possible avascular necrosis (bone death in the ball of the hip)
hip_knee:H5.sourceText:
H5 · Possible avascular necrosis (bone death in the ball of the hip)

CHECK: inward rotation of the hip (as in H3) — painful and limited in someone younger than is typical for arthritis?
NOTE: a younger patient with arthritis-like signs plus a risk factor needs imaging — early collapse of the bone changes management. Consensus; no bedside accuracy study. Check local sickle cell prevalence.

hip_knee:H6.title: H6 · Possible tumour, or cancer spread to bone

H6 · Possible tumour, or cancer spread to bone
ASK: History of cancer (breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid cancers often spread to bone)? Unexplained weight loss? Constant pain, worse at night and at rest, not changed by position?
NOTE: night pain ALONE is common in hip osteoarthritis. Escalate when night pain comes WITH constant pain, weight loss or a cancer history.
TEAM DATA: in the NAS records, night-pain patients were referred less often than average (4.7% vs 8.7%).

hip_knee:H7.title: H7 · Whole-body (inflammatory) or post-viral arthritis
hip_knee:H7.sourceText:
H7 · Whole-body (inflammatory) or post-viral arthritis
ASK: Morning stiffness over 60 minutes? Back or buttock pain that started before age 45, eases with exercise and wakes you in the second half of the night (inflammatory back pain)? Other swollen joints, psoriasis, bowel disease, a red painful eye? A high fever with rash before the joint pain (chikungunya)?
CHECK: count swollen joints — hands, wrists, knees, ankles, feet.
POSITIVE IF: 3 or more swollen joints, small-joint swelling, or an inflammatory back-pain pattern.
NOTE: axial spondyloarthritis (inflammatory arthritis of the spine and pelvis) often shows up as buttock or hip pain in young adults. About 25% of chikungunya cases develop long-lasting inflammatory joint disease (Rodriguez-Morales 2016).

H8 · Possible tuberculosis (TB) of the hip

CHECK: compare thigh and buttock size (wasting); is movement painful and limited?
NOTE: after the spine, the hip and knee are the commonest TB joints, mostly in younger people in TB-endemic areas (osteoarticular TB review, 2020).

CHECK: standing, look at the groin while they cough — a bulge or impulse? Then bend, rotate and load the hip — does that reproduce the pain?

H10 · Pain coming from the lower back

hip_knee:n5_719.title: SAFETY MODIFIERS — not stops; they change who signs off and how hard you start
hip_knee:n5_719.sourceText:
SAFETY MODIFIERS — not stops; they change who signs off and how hard you start
• Chest pain, breathlessness or fainting with effort → doctor before progressive exercise.
• Blood pressure clearly uncontrolled → doctor sign-off (local cut-off).
• Recent falls or poor balance → start with supported exercise and add a falls check (Timed Up-and-Go).
• Osteoporosis risk (older women, long steroid use) → no high-impact work until assessed.

CONTEXT TO RECORD (changes the plan)
• Underweight is common here (median BMI 18.8 in the NAS data); weight-loss advice often doesn’t apply.
• Cross-legged floor sitting, squatting toilets, rising from the floor and field work push the hip into deep bending and rotation. These define both the goals and the positions that may aggravate.
• Fear of movement, low mood and poor sleep slow recovery; handle them in education.

hip_knee:KS3.sourceText:
STAGE 3 — MEASURE, DOSE THE EXERCISE, RE-TEST
Every working diagnosis from Stage 2 comes here. Everyone gets the same short core battery so results compare across patients and visits; the diagnosis adds one module; irritability (not the label) sets the starting dose.

hip_knee:KS3-1.title: KS3-1 · How irritable is the knee?
hip_knee:KS3-1.sourceText:
KS3-1 · How irritable is the knee?
ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours too.

fields.ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours too.

options.label: HIGH: pain at rest or at night; flares with small movements; takes hours or until the next day to settle
MODERATE: pain with specific loads (stairs, squatting); settles within an hour or two
LOW: pain only at high load or at the end of activity; settles within minutes

hip_knee:KS3-HI.title: START GENTLE
hip_knee:KS3-HI.sourceText:
START GENTLE
Isometric holds, pain-free range of motion, walking in short bouts, education. Baseline limited to pain, the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) and range of motion.

fields.BODY: Isometric holds, pain-free range of motion, walking in short bouts, education. Baseline limited to pain, the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) and range of motion.

hip_knee:KS3-MD.title: START MODERATE
hip_knee:KS3-MD.sourceText:
START MODERATE
Progressive strengthening and practice of real tasks within the pain rule. Full core battery.

fields.BODY: Progressive strengthening and practice of real tasks within the pain rule. Full core battery.

hip_knee:KS3-LO.title: START STRONGER
hip_knee:KS3-LO.sourceText:
START STRONGER
Heavier loading, single-leg work, and hopping or sport tasks where relevant. Full core battery.

fields.BODY: Heavier loading, single-leg work, and hopping or sport tasks where relevant. Full core battery.

hip_knee:KS3-2.title: KS3-2 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes)
hip_knee:KS3-2.sourceText:
KS3-2 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes)
Needs: a chair, a stopwatch, 10 m of floor, a step and a phone. Repeat the SAME set at week 0, 4 and 12.
1. Pain 0–10 (faces version for low literacy): average and worst in the last week.
2. Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS): the patient names their 3 hardest tasks and rates each 0–10 — this becomes the goal list. Prompt with local tasks: floor sitting and rising, squatting toilet, stairs, kneeling for prayer, carrying water, field work.
3. 30-second chair stand: fixed-height chair, arms crossed, count full stands in 30 s (leg strength).
4. 40 m fast-paced walk: 4 × 10 m as fast as safely possible, timed.
5. Stair climb: time up and down one flight (note the number of steps).
6. Knee range of motion: phone inclinometer app or goniometer (angle ruler); heel-to-buttock distance if neither.
7. Straight-leg raise: does the knee sag as the leg lifts (quadriceps lag)?
8. Single-leg stance: up to 30 s each side (balance).
9. Gait video: 10 s phone video from the front and side.
Tests 3–5 are the core set recommended by OARSI, the Osteoarthritis Research Society International (Dobson 2013).

hip_knee:KS3-3.title: KS3-3 · ADD-ON MODULE — pick the one that matches the working diagnosis
hip_knee:KS3-3.sourceText:
KS3-3 · ADD-ON MODULE — pick the one that matches the working diagnosis
Osteoarthritis module (KD8, KD12, KD13, KD15): KOOS-12 or WOMAC questionnaire (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score / Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index — check for a validated Marathi or Hindi version); Timed Up-and-Go; optional 6-minute walk.
Injury module (KD1–KD4): IKDC form (International Knee Documentation Committee) or KOOS; swelling check; quadriceps strength side to side (handheld dynamometer, or single-leg sit-to-stand count); hop tests once pain-free running is possible; ACL-RSI (fear of re-injury questionnaire).
Kneecap module (KD5, KD9, KD11, KD16): Kujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale; step-down pain; hip abductor and extensor strength (side-lying hold time if no dynamometer).
Tendon module (KD10): VISA-P (Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment — patellar tendon); single-leg decline squat pain 0–10.
Growing-knee module (KD6): weekly activity log; kneeling and jumping pain 0–10.

hip_knee:n5_567.title: PAIN RULE FOR HOME EXERCISE
hip_knee:n5_567.sourceText:
PAIN RULE FOR HOME EXERCISE
Pain up to about 5 out of 10 during exercise is acceptable if it has settled back to its usual level by the next morning. If not, hold or step down one level. Warn patients that pain may rise a little at first (NICE NG226).

hip_knee:n5_522.title: WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T)
hip_knee:n5_522.sourceText:
WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T)
For osteoarthritis and degenerative meniscus tears the exercise plan is basically the same shared core programme. For patellar tendinopathy, kneecap pain and ACL injury, the label changes the plan a lot. So the diagnosis should pick the programme module, the dose and the positions to avoid — not a custom exercise list per patient.

hip_knee:KD1.title: KD1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: ACL injury (torn anterior cruciate ligament)
hip_knee:KD1.sourceText:
KD1 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: ACL injury (torn anterior cruciate ligament)
WHAT IT IS: the ligament that stops the shin sliding forward is torn; the knee may give way when turning.
NEXT STEP — rehab first: control swelling, regain full straightening, wake up the thigh muscle; then heavy quadriceps and hamstring strength, balance, landing and cutting practice. Return to sport by strength and hop tests, not by time. In the KANON trial, rehab with optional later surgery did as well as early surgery at 2 and 5 years, and about half of the rehab group never needed surgery (Frobell 2010, 2013).
AVOID: pivoting sport before strength and hop tests are close to the other side.
REFER (surgical opinion) IF: the knee keeps giving way in daily life despite good rehab.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: injury module.

hip_knee:KN1.title: KN1 · Can’t clear the ACL yet
hip_knee:KN1.sourceText:
KN1 · Can’t clear the ACL yet
A swollen, guarded knee hides ligament looseness. Protect it, control the swelling, start gentle range and thigh-muscle tightening, and RE-TEST in 1–2 weeks (back to KT1).

fields.BODY: A swollen, guarded knee hides ligament looseness. Protect it, control the swelling, start gentle range and thigh-muscle tightening, and RE-TEST in 1–2 weeks (back to KT1).

hip_knee:KT1.title: KT1 · Test the ACL (anterior cruciate ligament — the main ligament that stops the shin bone sliding forward)
hip_knee:KT1.sourceText:
KT1 · Test the ACL (anterior cruciate ligament — the main ligament that stops the shin bone sliding forward)
• Lachman test: knee bent 20–30°, steady the thigh with one hand, pull the shin forward with the other; compare sides. Extra movement or a soft end-point = positive. Sensitivity 85%, specificity 94% (Benjaminse 2006); 81% / 85% in a 2022 meta-analysis (Sokal 2022).
• Lever sign: patient lying flat; put a fist under the upper calf and press down on the thigh just above the kneecap. The heel should lift — heel stays down = positive. Sensitivity 83%, specificity 91% (Sokal 2022). Easier for a small examiner or a large leg.
• Pivot shift (relaxed patient only): very specific (94–98%) but often missed when the patient guards.
WHO: physio-level

options.label: Lachman OR lever sign positive

Both clearly negative in a relaxed knee → check the meniscus (KT2)

hip_knee:KD2.title: KD2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Traumatic meniscus tear
hip_knee:KD2.sourceText:
KD2 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Traumatic meniscus tear
WHAT IT IS: one of the two C-shaped cartilage cushions between the thigh bone and shin bone is torn by a twist.
NEXT STEP: settle swelling and restore full straightening first; then closed-chain strength (sit-to-stand, step-ups, mini squats); then single-leg control, pivoting, and return to work or sport tasks (JOSPT meniscus guideline, Logerstedt 2018).
AVOID: deep loaded squats and pivoting while it still swells after activity.
REFER IF: true locking (K6), or catching that blocks progress by week 4–6. Without imaging you can’t tell a repairable tear from a non-repairable one.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: injury module.

hip_knee:KT2.title: KT2 · Meniscus check — count how many of these 5 are positive (Lowery composite)
hip_knee:KT2.sourceText:
KT2 · Meniscus check — count how many of these 5 are positive (Lowery composite)
1. History of catching or locking
2. Pain when the knee is pushed fully straight (forced hyperextension)
3. Pain at full bend (maximum flexion)
4. Pain or a click on the McMurray test (bend fully, twist the shin in and out, then straighten)
5. Tenderness when pressing along the joint line (the gap between thigh bone and shin bone)
EVIDENCE: with all 5 positive, 92% had a meniscus tear; with 3 or more, over 75% did when there was no ACL tear or arthritis (Lowery 2006, 635 knees). Single tests are weak: McMurray sensitivity 61% / specificity 84%; joint-line tenderness 83% / 83%; Thessaly test at 20° 75% / 87% (Smith 2015 meta-analysis).
WHO: physio-level

hip_knee:KD3.title: KD3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: MCL or LCL sprain (side-ligament sprain)
hip_knee:KD3.sourceText:
KD3 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: MCL or LCL sprain (side-ligament sprain)
WHAT IT IS: a stretched or partly torn ligament on the inner (MCL) or outer (LCL) side.
NEXT STEP: movement from week 1, then progressive strengthening and functional loading; a hinged brace for more severe MCL sprains (JOSPT ligament guideline 2017).
AVOID: side-to-side stress and pivoting until the stress test is pain-free.
REFER IF: gapping with the knee straight (KX1), or in a child (possible growth-plate injury).
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: injury module.

hip_knee:KX1.title: URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
hip_knee:KX1.sourceText:
URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
Likely combined ligament injury. Brace and refer to orthopaedics.

fields.BODY: Likely combined ligament injury. Brace and refer to orthopaedics.

hip_knee:KT3.title: KT3 · Side-ligament check — MCL (medial collateral ligament, inner side) and LCL (lateral collateral ligament, outer side)
hip_knee:KT3.sourceText:
KT3 · Side-ligament check — MCL (medial collateral ligament, inner side) and LCL (lateral collateral ligament, outer side)
• Push the knee inward (valgus stress — tests the MCL) and outward (varus stress — tests the LCL), first with the knee bent 30°, then fully straight (0°).
• Feel along the ligament from thigh bone to shin bone.
POSITIVE IF: pain or gapping at 30° = an isolated sprain. Gapping with the knee fully straight = more than one structure is torn. Tender along the ligament (not on the joint line) supports a sprain.
EVIDENCE: recommended in the JOSPT knee ligament guideline (Logerstedt 2017); no strong accuracy figures — grading is by feel.
WHO: physio-level (stress tests); anyone trained (pressing)

• Feel along the ligament from thigh bone to shin bone.

hip_knee:KD4.title: KD4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: PCL injury (torn posterior cruciate ligament)
hip_knee:KD4.sourceText:
KD4 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: PCL injury (torn posterior cruciate ligament)
WHAT IT IS: the ligament that stops the shin sliding backward is torn; often vague pain at the back of the knee with little swelling.
NEXT STEP: quadriceps-led rehab with a brace in the early phase; gradual return to kneeling and squatting (JOSPT ligament guideline 2017).
AVOID: resisted hamstring curls early on — they pull the shin backward.
REFER IF: a combined injury is suspected, or the knee feels unstable when twisting.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: injury module.

hip_knee:KT4.title: KT4 · Back-ligament check — PCL (posterior cruciate ligament — stops the shin sliding backward)
hip_knee:KT4.sourceText:
KT4 · Back-ligament check — PCL (posterior cruciate ligament — stops the shin sliding backward)
• Posterior sag: lying down, both knees bent to 90° with feet flat; look from the side — does the injured shin sag backward?
• Posterior drawer: knee bent 90°, push the shin backward; compare with the other side.
EVIDENCE: clinical exam led by the posterior drawer: sensitivity 90%, specificity 99% (Rubinstein 1994; surgeon examiners, long-standing tears).
WHO: physio-level

• Posterior drawer: knee bent 90°, push the shin backward; compare with the other side.

hip_knee:KD5.title: KD5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: First-time kneecap (patellar) dislocation
hip_knee:KD5.sourceText:
KD5 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: First-time kneecap (patellar) dislocation
WHAT IT IS: the kneecap slid out to the outer side; it often pops back by itself.
NEXT STEP: X-ray every first dislocation to look for a broken-off fragment; a fragment → urgent knee specialist (BOAST 2024). Otherwise physiotherapy: quadriceps and hip strengthening, balance and landing control, taping or a brace for return to sport.
IF IT HAPPENS AGAIN: see KQ1 → “keeps giving way”.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: kneecap module.

hip_knee:KQ2.title: KQ2 · What happened at the moment of injury?
hip_knee:KQ2.sourceText:
KQ2 · What happened at the moment of injury?
ASK: “Show me or describe exactly how it happened, and what you felt and saw over the next day.”
NOTE: fracture (K1) must already be cleared.

fields.ASK: “Show me or describe exactly how it happened, and what you felt and saw over the next day.”
fields.NOTE: fracture (K1) must already be cleared.

options.label: Twisted or landed, felt or heard a POP, swelled within a few hours, couldn’t carry on
Twisted on a bent, loaded knee; swelling crept up over the next day; now it catches
Hit or pushed on the SIDE of the knee; pain on the inner or outer side
Fell onto a bent knee, or the shin hit a dashboard
The kneecap slid out to the side (it may have popped back)

hip_knee:KD6.title: KD6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Osgood-Schlatter (top of the shin) or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson (bottom tip of the kneecap)
hip_knee:KD6.sourceText:
KD6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Osgood-Schlatter (top of the shin) or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson (bottom tip of the kneecap)
WHAT IT IS: irritation of a growth plate where the kneecap tendon pulls, in sporty children during a growth spurt.
CONFIRM: pressing the bump is tender, often swollen; worse with kneeling, jumping and stairs.
NEXT STEP: reduce jumping and kneeling volume but keep the child active; quadriceps and hip strength, calf and thigh flexibility; a kneeling pad. Usually settles with growth (consensus).
AVOID: total rest from all sport; injections.
RED FLAG: constant or night pain → K9.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: growing-knee module.

hip_knee:KD7.title: KD7 · REFER FOR IMAGING: suspected osteochondritis dissecans
hip_knee:KD7.sourceText:
KD7 · REFER FOR IMAGING: suspected osteochondritis dissecans
WHAT IT IS: a patch of bone under the joint cartilage loses its blood supply and can loosen; seen in active teenagers.
WHY REFER: it cannot be diagnosed without an X-ray — this is where a no-imaging pathway must hand off.
MEANWHILE: reduce jumping and running; keep thigh strength (consensus).

hip_knee:KQ4.title: KQ4 · Child: where does it hurt?
hip_knee:KQ4.sourceText:
KQ4 · Child: where does it hurt?
ASK: “Point with one finger.”
FIRST: make sure the hip has been checked (K8) — hip problems in children often show up as knee pain.

hip_knee:KD9.title: KD9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Patellofemoral pain (pain from the joint behind the kneecap)
hip_knee:KD9.sourceText:
KD9 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Patellofemoral pain (pain from the joint behind the kneecap)
WHAT IT IS: overload of the joint between the kneecap and the thigh bone; common in active teenagers and young adults.
NEXT STEP: hip and knee strengthening is the core treatment — hip abductors and extensors plus quadriceps, high volume where tolerated (about 3 sets of 30+ repetitions, 3 times a week); short-term kneecap taping or off-the-shelf foot insoles as add-ons; change squat depth and stair habits rather than stopping activity (Willy 2019; Crossley 2016 consensus).
AVOID: knee braces or sleeves; passive treatments on their own.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: kneecap module.

hip_knee:KT6.title: KT6 · Kneecap-pain check (patellofemoral pain)
hip_knee:KT6.sourceText:
KT6 · Kneecap-pain check (patellofemoral pain)
• Squat: slow double-leg squat as deep as comfortable. Does it reproduce their front-of-knee pain? This is the most useful single sign — NO pain on squatting makes this diagnosis unlikely (JOSPT guideline, Willy 2019).
• Typical history: pain with stairs (especially going down), kneeling, and long sitting with the knees bent.
• Step-down or single-leg squat: film from the front — pain; knee drifts inward; hip drops.
WHO: anyone trained

• Step-down or single-leg squat: film from the front — pain; knee drifts inward; hip drops.

options.label: Squatting reproduces the pain
Squat is pain-free → recheck the spot (KT7)

hip_knee:KD10.title: KD10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Patellar tendinopathy (“jumper’s knee”)
hip_knee:KD10.sourceText:
KD10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Patellar tendinopathy (“jumper’s knee”)
WHAT IT IS: the tendon just below the kneecap is overloaded and sensitive.
NEXT STEP — staged tendon loading: (1) isometric holds such as a wall sit for pain relief → (2) heavy slow strength (squats, leg press) → (3) energy storage (jumps, hops) added slowly → (4) full sport or work. Track decline-squat pain daily: it shouldn’t climb from one day to the next. Rehab often takes months (Malliaras 2015).
AVOID: complete rest; passive treatments as the main plan; big jumps in jumping volume.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: tendon module.

hip_knee:KT7.title: KT7 · Kneecap-tendon check (patellar tendinopathy)
hip_knee:KT7.sourceText:
KT7 · Kneecap-tendon check (patellar tendinopathy)
• Press the bottom edge of the kneecap with the knee straight and relaxed — tender at one spot?
• Single-leg decline squat (on a 25° slope): pain at the tendon that rises with depth (physio-level).
• Typical history: jumping, running or heavy squatting; the pain warms up during activity, then returns afterwards and the next day.
HALLMARKS: pain at the bottom tip of the kneecap + pain that rises with load on the thigh muscle (Malliaras 2015). Diagnosis stays clinical: tendon changes on scans are common in pain-free athletes.
WHO: anyone trained (press); physio-level (decline squat)

hip_knee:KD11.title: KD11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome
hip_knee:KD11.sourceText:
KD11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome
WHAT IT IS: irritation where the thick band of tissue on the outer thigh crosses the knee.
NEXT STEP: reduce running volume and downhill work for a period; strengthen the hip abductors; return gradually with changes to cadence (step rate) or route (consensus-level evidence).
AVOID: running through sharp outer-knee pain.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: kneecap module (step-down pain, hip strength).

hip_knee:KT8.title: KT8 · Outer-knee check
hip_knee:KT8.sourceText:
KT8 · Outer-knee check
• History: running, cycling or long walks, with pain coming on at a predictable distance?
• Press the bony outer knee just above the joint line (lateral femoral epicondyle) — tender?
• Noble compression (physio-level): press that spot while bending and straightening the knee — pain near 30° of bend.
• Tender ON the joint line instead, with catching? → meniscus check (KT2).
EVIDENCE: consensus; no validated accuracy figures.
WHO: anyone trained; physio-level (Noble)

hip_knee:KD12.title: KD12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Degenerative meniscus tear
hip_knee:KD12.sourceText:
KD12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Degenerative meniscus tear
WHAT IT IS: age-related wear of the inner cartilage cushion, often alongside early osteoarthritis.
NEXT STEP: treat like knee osteoarthritis — supervised progressive exercise for about 12 weeks before any talk of surgery. In a trial of 140 middle-aged adults, 12 weeks of exercise matched keyhole surgery (arthroscopic partial meniscectomy) at 2 years (Kise 2016).
AVOID: referral for keyhole surgery as first-line care.
REFER IF: true locking appears (K6).
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: osteoarthritis module.

hip_knee:KD13.title: KD13 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Pes anserine pain
hip_knee:KD13.sourceText:
KD13 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Pes anserine pain
WHAT IT IS: a tender spot on the inner shin where three tendons attach, just below the knee; often alongside osteoarthritis.
NEXT STEP: the osteoarthritis core programme plus hamstring and hip strengthening; a pillow between the knees at night (consensus).
AVOID: injection as the first plan.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: osteoarthritis module.

hip_knee:KT9.title: KT9 · Inner-side check
hip_knee:KT9.sourceText:
KT9 · Inner-side check
• Press the joint line with the knee bent 90° (the gap between thigh bone and shin bone on the inner side).
• Press the inner shin a few centimetres BELOW the joint line (where three tendons attach — the pes anserine).
• History: middle-aged; little or no injury (e.g. getting up from a squat); catching that frees itself?
WHO: anyone trained (press); physio-level (meniscus tests, KT2)

hip_knee:KD14.title: KD14 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Prepatellar bursitis (“housemaid’s knee”)
hip_knee:KD14.sourceText:
KD14 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Prepatellar bursitis (“housemaid’s knee”)
WHAT IT IS: an irritated fluid sac on top of the kneecap from kneeling pressure (work, floor cleaning, farming, prayer).
NEXT STEP: a kneeling pad or a change in kneeling posture; keep thigh strength; treat any joint problem underneath (consensus).
AVOID: repeated direct kneeling on the swelling.

hip_knee:KX2.title: EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
hip_knee:KX2.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
Possible infected bursa: doctor today (see K3).

hip_knee:KT10.title: KT10 · Swelling on top of the kneecap — is it infected?
hip_knee:KT10.sourceText:
KT10 · Swelling on top of the kneecap — is it infected?
• Can you feel the edges of the kneecap through the swelling, and does the knee still bend fairly freely? (Yes to both = the swelling is in a fluid sac on top of the kneecap, not inside the joint.)
• Is it hot or red, with fever or a skin break?
WHO: basic kit (thermometer)

options.label: Not hot, no fever

hip_knee:KD15.title: KD15 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Baker’s (popliteal) cyst
hip_knee:KD15.sourceText:
KD15 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Baker’s (popliteal) cyst
WHAT IT IS: a fluid sac behind the knee, usually caused by osteoarthritis or a meniscus problem inside the joint.
CONFIRM: soft swelling at the back of the knee, more obvious when standing or with the knee straight.
NEXT STEP: treat the joint problem underneath — usually the osteoarthritis core programme (consensus).
DANGER SIGN: a sudden painful, swollen calf = possible rupture or blood clot → K4 same day.

hip_knee:KQ5.title: KQ5 · Where does it hurt?
hip_knee:KQ5.sourceText:
KQ5 · Where does it hurt?
ASK: “Point with one finger to the sorest spot.” Then look at it and press there.

One spot at the bottom edge of the kneecap
Outer side of the knee

hip_knee:KD8.title: KD8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Knee osteoarthritis (OA)
hip_knee:KD8.sourceText:
KD8 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Knee osteoarthritis (OA)
WHAT IT IS: “wear and repair” changes in the joint’s cartilage and bone — the most common cause of knee pain from mid-life on. Diagnosed from symptoms; X-ray changes match pain poorly and don’t change first-line care.
NEXT STEP: education + strengthening + balance (neuromuscular) exercise is the core treatment (NICE NG226; OARSI 2019) — e.g. the GLA:D programme: 2 education sessions + 12 supervised exercise sessions over 6–8 weeks (Skou & Roos 2017). Build up walking in bouts; a walking stick if it keeps them active; practise their own goal tasks (rising from the floor, squatting to a set depth).
AVOID: passive treatments on their own (electrotherapy, acupuncture, manual therapy), routine braces or insoles, imaging to plan care, “lose weight” advice for an underweight patient.
OFTEN ALONGSIDE (same programme): degenerative meniscus tear, pes anserine pain, Baker’s cyst.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: osteoarthritis module.

hip_knee:KT5.title: KT5 · Osteoarthritis check (no X-ray needed)
hip_knee:KT5.sourceText:
KT5 · Osteoarthritis check (no X-ray needed)
NICE clinical diagnosis — all three: age 45 or older ✓ • pain with activity (walking, stairs, squatting, rising from the floor) that eases with rest • morning stiffness absent or 30 minutes or less (NICE NG226, 2022).
For extra confidence — ACR clinical criteria (American College of Rheumatology): knee pain plus 3 or more of: age over 50 • stiffness under 30 minutes • creaking or grating on movement (crepitus) • tenderness of the bone at the joint edges • bony enlargement • no warmth. 3 of 6: sensitivity 95%, specificity 69%; 4 of 6: 84% / 89% (Altman 1986).
WHO: anyone trained

hip_knee:KD16.title: KD16 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Recurrent kneecap instability
hip_knee:KD16.sourceText:
KD16 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Recurrent kneecap instability
NEXT STEP: quadriceps and hip strengthening as for kneecap pain (KD9), balance and landing control, taping or a brace for return to sport.
AVOID: deep pivoting before control returns.
REFER IF: repeated dislocations — the bony shape and cartilage damage need imaging.
STAGE 3 ADD-ON: kneecap module.

• J-sign: watch the kneecap as the seated patient straightens the knee — it jumps sideways near full straightening.
• History: often teenage girls, loose joints, family history.
EVIDENCE: consensus; no strong accuracy figures.
WHO: physio-level

hip_knee:KT12.title: KT12 · Old ACL tear check
hip_knee:KT12.sourceText:
KT12 · Old ACL tear check
Run KT1 (Lachman and lever sign) plus the anterior drawer: knee bent 90°, foot steadied, pull the shin forward and compare sides. In long-standing tears the anterior drawer has sensitivity 92% and specificity 91%; it is much weaker in fresh, swollen injuries (Benjaminse 2006).
WHO: physio-level

hip_knee:KN2.title: KN2 · Giving way from weakness or pain
hip_knee:KN2.sourceText:
KN2 · Giving way from weakness or pain
Pain switches off the thigh muscle, so the knee buckles even though nothing is torn — common in osteoarthritis and kneecap pain. Strengthening fixes it. Go to the osteoarthritis check (KT5) if 45+, otherwise the kneecap check (KT6).

hip_knee:KQ6.sourceText:

hip_knee:G-KNEE.sourceText:
KNEE PATHWAY
Stage 1 safety screen (13 checks) → Stage 2 which knee problem is it (16 working diagnoses) → Stage 3 measure, dose the exercise, re-test.

hip_knee:KS1.sourceText:
STAGE 1 — SAFETY SCREEN: Is this knee pain safe to treat with exercise?
Ask the 13 checks in order, most time-critical first. Any YES stops the pathway and names the action. All NO → Stage 2. “Exercise-responsive” is decided by ruling these out, then confirmed by improvement at the week-4 re-test (Stage 3).

hip_knee:K1.title: K1 · Possible broken bone (fracture)
hip_knee:K1.sourceText:
K1 · Possible broken bone (fracture)
ASK: Did the pain start with a fall, blow, twist or accident in the last 7 days? Could you walk straight afterwards?
CHECK — Ottawa Knee Rule (any ONE item = positive):
• age 55 or older
• tender ONLY over the kneecap (no other bony tenderness)
• tender at the head of the fibula (the bony bump on the outer side, just below the knee)
• can’t bend the knee to 90°
• can’t take 4 steps, both right after the injury and now (limping steps count)
EVIDENCE: sensitivity about 98.5% (6 studies, 4,249 adults) — a negative rule makes a fracture very unlikely. Specificity is low (about 49%) on purpose: the job here is to miss nothing (Bachmann 2004).
WHO: anyone trained

hip_knee:K1Y.title: EMERGENCY
hip_knee:K1Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY
Splint the knee, no weight-bearing exercise, same-day X-ray through the doctor.

hip_knee:K2.title: K2 · Dislocated knee, or damage to the artery or nerve
hip_knee:K2.sourceText:
K2 · Dislocated knee, or damage to the artery or nerve
ASK: High-energy injury (road accident, fall from a height)? Did the knee look out of place? Is the foot cold, pale, numb, tingling or weak? Is the pain far worse than the injury looks, with a tight, swollen calf (possible compartment syndrome — dangerous pressure build-up inside the muscle)?
CHECK: feel the foot pulses (top of the foot, and behind the inner ankle bone) and compare sides. Press a toenail and compare how fast the pink colour returns with the other foot. Light touch on the top and sole of the foot; wiggle the toes; lift the foot up.
POSITIVE IF: weaker pulse, slow colour return, cold foot, numbness or foot drop.
NOTE: a dislocated knee can pop back in by itself and still have a torn artery. Standard emergency teaching (consensus; no bedside accuracy study).
WHO: anyone trained

hip_knee:K2Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY
Emergency transfer now. Do not wait for the knee to settle.

hip_knee:K3.title: K3 · Hot, red, swollen knee — possible joint infection (septic arthritis) or gout
hip_knee:K3.sourceText:
K3 · Hot, red, swollen knee — possible joint infection (septic arthritis) or gout
ASK: Did it swell up quickly over hours to days without a clear injury? Fever, chills, feeling unwell? Recent injection into the knee, a skin wound, diabetes, steroid use or a weak immune system? Past attacks like this (gout)?
CHECK: temperature. Back of the hand on both knees — is one clearly warmer? Look for swelling that fills the dimples beside the kneecap. Can they stand on it and bend it?
EVIDENCE: fever is present in only 57% of joint infections — a normal temperature does NOT clear this check (Margaretten 2007). Gout and pseudogout look the same at the bedside; only drawing fluid from the joint tells them apart.
WHO: basic kit (thermometer)

hip_knee:K3Y.sourceText:
EMERGENCY — SAME DAY
Treat as a joint infection until proven otherwise. Same-day doctor to draw fluid from the joint (aspiration). No exercise.

hip_knee:K4.title: K4 · Possible blood clot in the leg (deep vein thrombosis, DVT)
hip_knee:K4.sourceText:
K4 · Possible blood clot in the leg (deep vein thrombosis, DVT)
ASK: Calf pain or swelling? Recent surgery, a plaster cast, bed rest or a long journey? Cancer, pregnancy, hormone pills or a past clot?
CHECK (items from the Wells score): measure both calves 10 cm below the bony bump under the kneecap and compare; pitting swelling (press — does a dent stay?); tenderness along the deep veins at the back of the calf and inner thigh; is the whole leg swollen?
NOTE: the Wells score itself is calculated by the doctor (Wells 1997). A burst Baker’s cyst (fluid sac behind the knee) can look identical and needs the same check.
WHO: basic kit (tape measure)

Doctor to score the risk and arrange an ultrasound scan or a D-dimer blood test. No exercise until cleared.

hip_knee:K5.title: K5 · Can’t straighten the knee against gravity — torn quadriceps or kneecap tendon
hip_knee:K5.sourceText:
K5 · Can’t straighten the knee against gravity — torn quadriceps or kneecap tendon
ASK: After a stumble or awkward landing, did something give way at the front of the knee? Can you lift your leg straight off the bed?
CHECK: lying on the back, lift the leg with the knee fully straight (active straight-leg raise). Feel above and below the kneecap for a gap; compare kneecap height with the other side.
POSITIVE IF: can’t lift it, or the knee sags as the leg lifts (extension lag); a gap; the kneecap sits too high or too low.
NOTE: a good straight-leg raise makes this unlikely (consensus; no accuracy study).
WHO: anyone trained

hip_knee:K5Y.title: URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
hip_knee:K5Y.sourceText:
URGENT — WITHIN DAYS
Orthopaedics (bone and joint specialist): repair is time-sensitive. Brace the knee straight meanwhile.

hip_knee:K6.title: K6 · Truly locked knee
hip_knee:K6.sourceText:
K6 · Truly locked knee
ASK: Is the knee stuck bent so it won’t straighten at all, even with help? Or does it catch and then free itself?
CHECK: ask them to relax, then gently try to straighten the knee.
POSITIVE IF: a firm block short of straight (not just pain).
NOTE: true locking suggests a torn flap of cartilage stuck in the joint (e.g. a “bucket-handle” meniscus tear). Brief catching that frees itself does NOT stop the pathway — it is a clue for Stage 2 (consensus).
WHO: anyone trained
